detail.abstract: Transparency protects investors by reducing information asymmetry, strengthening fiduciary monitoring, and improving the pricing of risk. Yet in high-accountability investment portfolios, transparency is often treated as a reporting output rather than a governance operating system. This paper synthesizes research on disclosure, agency costs, and information risk to explain how transparency changes investor outcomes and why disclosure volume can fail to produce decision-useful clarity. Using a structured literature review and a governance-to-reporting mapping method, the paper identifies five transparency mechanisms: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, usability, and accountability response. Results are summarized in an integrated framework that links each mechanism to expected effects on liquidity, cost of capital, and fraud or misstatement risk. The paper proposes a layered transparency model for high-accountability portfolios that combines standardized classification, narrative drivers, structured data, and escalation protocols aligned to internal control frameworks such as COSO. The analysis concludes that investor protection improves when transparency is designed to enable replicable oversight across entities and reporting cycles, supported by credible assurance and remediation pathways.

detail.abstract: We introduce a novel methodology, ”parametric tilting,” for incorporating external information into econometric model-based density forecasts. Unlike traditional entropic tilting, which can generate unrealistic or unstable distributions under certain conditions, parametric tilting ensures more reliable and numerically stable results. Our approach leverages the flexibility of the skew-T distribution, which captures key moments of macroeconomic time series, and minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the target and model-based distributions. This method overcomes limitations of entropic tilting, such as multimodal or degenerate distributions, providing a robust alternative for policymakers and researchers aiming to integrate external views into probabilistic forecasting frameworks.

This paper develops a novel Poisson detection model leveraging high-frequency dining-card transaction data from a Chinese university to reconstruct a large-scale social network, identifying tens of thousands of friend pairs within millions of dyads. We find a significant asymmetry in friendship formation: while local students residing with nonlocal peers show an increased propensity to form friendships with individuals from that specific province, nonlocal students do not exhibit a reciprocal effect. We attribute this phenomenon to an experiential learning mechanism governed by informational gradients: daily exposure most effectively reshapes stereotypes when the outgroup member belongs to a numerically smaller group, where the marginal value of information is highest.

detail.abstract: We investigate China's influence at the United Nations by focusing on the promotion of its narratives (words) and its voting behaviour (deeds). For the former, we assess the extent to which China's global initiatives have become embedded in UN discourse compared to Western initiatives. For the latter, we assess the degree to which countries, regions and voting coalitions align their UN General Assembly votes with China compared to the US. When it comes to words, China's global initiatives are sometimes louder than the West's. More specifically, the Belt and Road Initiative has had a much greater impact on UN discourse than any Western initiative. Other Chinese global initiatives do not clearly stand out from those of the West, with the Global Compact for Migration mentioned more frequently at the UN than any Chinese initiative other than the BRI. We also find that Chinese initiatives are more self-referential. Thematically, both Chinese and Western initiatives are very focused on security as well as aid and human rights. Moving to voting patterns, countries' income levels are a key determinant of alignment in voting. Poorer countries are much more aligned with China than with the US. North America and the European Union, in that order, are generally more aligned with the US than with China and these trends are much more stable than one could expect given China's growing economic influence.

detail.abstract: The accurate estimation of catastrophe tail risk-specifically Value at Risk (VaR) and Tail Value at Risk (TVaR) at extreme percentiles-poses a profound computational challenge for the global reinsurance industry. Traditional classical Monte Carlo (MC) simulations suffer from high estimator variance and severe sample inefficiency when modeling low-probability, high-severity events. In this paper, we introduce a hybrid quantum-classical simulation architecture designed to reduce estimator variance and optimize non-proportional reinsurance layer structures. Our system integrates physicsbased classical catastrophe modeling with Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) and Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE) to efficiently sample heavy-tailed loss distributions. To bridge the gap between theoretical quantum speedups and Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware realities, our system introduces a dynamic backend scheduler driven by a multi-variable scoring function balancing precision, queue latency, and cost, alongside Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) for error mitigation. Furthermore, we present a Capital Efficiency (𝐶𝐸) objective function used for portfolio optimization. Experimental benchmarks on a synthetic coastal hurricane portfolio demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves tail precision equivalent to approximately 2.0 × 10 ! classical Monte Carlo samples using only 7.5 × 10 " quantum shots-a 96.25% reduction in sample complexity-yielding a 35% reduction in estimator variance at the 99.5th percentile.

detail.abstract: This paper defines arbitrage as the systematic exploitation of structural asymmetries to extract economic value disproportionate to value created, further extending the concept of financial arbitrage to encompass systematic value extraction through non-market asymmetries in economics. This paper establishes five foundational criteria that distinguishes non-financial arbitrage from mere opportunism or fraud, structural asymmetry, disproportionate value extraction, economic manifestation, systematic replicability, and resistance to elimination. title: Updating the EU strategy on China: Co-existence while Derisking through Partnerships

detail.title: Updating the EU strategy on China: Co-existence while Derisking through Partnerships
detail.abstract:
Executive summary

The European Union-China relationship has deteriorated markedly since the EU introduced a three-part strategy in 2019 based on partnership, competition and systemic rivalry. Th e relationship has been undermined by China’s support for Russia’s aggression in Ukraine and its increasingly anti-Western foreign policy that aims to alter the international rules-based system. Meanwhile, the economic relationship is changing because of China’s structural deceleration and increasing self-reliance, coupled with the EU’s growing critical dependence on China, especially for digitalisation and decarbonisation. Europe must accept that relations with China will not return to their pre-pandemic state. 

While there is no need to change the overall strategy, the EU should seek co-existence with China while preserving EU values and interests. Cooperation is still needed to address global problems, including climate change, in which China plays an important role in finding solutions, but on which the EU cannot accept Chinese cooperation at any price. 

In terms of co-existence, the EU must continue to pursue de-risking – or reducing its exposure to China – especially for its energy and digital transitions. De-risking has started but more needs to be done to understand how it can be continued while not creating conflict. 

The EU should pursue a three-part approach: increase coherence and coordination with all European stakeholders, refi ne the EU economic-security strategy while accepting trade-offs and seek partnerships as the best offensive tool. The 2024-2029 European Commission should foster discussion of China and coordination of strategic issues within a larger constituency. EU countries, with Commission coordination, need to be more involved in building a comprehensive approach, including by conducting national risk assessments and by shaping and implementing de-risking measures. 

On economic security, full implementation of current defensive instruments is needed, along with new protections, such as better coordination of export controls and a new outbound-investment screening mechanism. The trade-off s stemming from pursuing more security will need to be made explicit in order to mitigate them. 

On partnerships, the EU must look beyond the United States, working within the G7 and with other like-minded countries, such as Australia and South Korea, which have valuable experience of de-risking. Mutually beneficial and strategic cooperation agreements need to be brokered with relevant emerging and developing economies.

detail.abstract: Did you know, Every year billions of dollars in social benefits go unclaimed every year by people who are legally entitled to them. What if this persistent gap in benefit take up represents a strategic trade off between the citizen's participation costs and the government's budgetary constraints? This paper presents an argument that underutilisation is a Strategic Dysfunction. Using two models, the paper will demonstrate that participation costs act as a filter for the individual and a fiscal safety net for the government.

title: How Does Competition Affect Firms’ Carbon Performance? Firm-Level Evidence from Tariff Cuts
affiliations: University of Augsburg, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Augsburg and University of St. Gallen - School of Finance

detail.title: How Does Competition Affect Firms’ Carbon Performance? Firm-Level Evidence from Tariff Cuts
detail.abstract: We examine how changes in competition affect firms’ carbon performance. Exploiting reductions in import tariffs as a quasi-natural experiment that increases competitive pressure, we find that stronger competition improves firms’ carbon efficiency through lower Scope 1 and 2 emission intensities. These results remain robust to alternative specifications, heterogeneous treatment effects, and placebo tests. Mechanism analyses indicate systematic differences in firms’ strategic responses. High-emission-intensity firms tend to adopt visible environmental actions and reallocate resources toward intangible assets, whereas low-emission firms increase investment and internal financing activities. Overall, our results highlight competition as a determinant of corporate decarbonization, suggesting that market forces can complement regulatory approaches to improving firms’ environmental performance.

title: Investor Attention and Stock Returns under Collusive Trading
affiliations: Hanyang University - School of  Business and Hanyang University

detail.title: Investor Attention and Stock Returns under Collusive Trading
detail.abstract: We investigate the effect of investor attention on stock return under the setting of collusive trading. Using a unique case of collusive trading, a type of stock price manipulation, this paper shows that the positive link between investor attention and stock returns disappears under collusive trading. Prior to the period of collusive trading, investor attention influences stock returns as expected, but collusive trades break this linkage. Comparisons with price run-up stocks and propensity score-matched stocks confirm that this disruption occurs only to stocks of collusive trading. Difference-in-Difference and placebo tests indicate that collusive trading drives these effects. These findings suggest that monitoring investor attention can serve as an early warning for a special form of stock price manipulation, providing a practical tool for market surveillance.

title: Oil Price and Sectoral Volatility Spillovers
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Oil Price and Sectoral Volatility Spillovers

keywords.keywords: Oil Price Volatility: Intraday Spillovers: Sectoral Stock Indices: Volatility Connectedness: High-Frequency Data: Oil-Importing and Exporting Economies

detail.abstract: This research looks at the spillovers of intraday volatility. From crude oil prices to sectoral stock indices across major oil-importing and oil-exporting economies. Using high-frequency data collected at 5-minute intervals from July 31, 2020, to April 30, 2021—a period marked by considerable uncertainty due to the global health crisis—the analysis covers five oil-exporting nations and nine oil-importing nations. Ten sectoral indices that capture complex market dynamics are hand-constructed from a sample of 1,689 individual stocks.Based on the data, overall volatility connectedness remains very high after the pandemic’s severe market volatility. Although the strength and direction of these spillovers differ greatly across nations and sectors, there are robust and fluctuating volatility transmission patterns between oil prices and sector indices. In the UK and Norway, oil prices are the main net transmitters of volatility across sectors. On the flip side, oil is primarily a market beneficiary when it comes to the volatility of the US and Canadian sector indices. On the other hand, the correlations between oil price volatility and sectoral markets in South Korea, China, Mexico, and Australia are relatively weak. Findings stress the importance of sector- and country-specific characteristics in impacting volatility transmission mechanisms and the varied character of oil-stock market interactions.

title: Friends and Defaults in a Third Party Dictator Experiment
affiliations: University of California, Merced

detail.title: Friends and Defaults in a Third Party Dictator Experiment
detail.abstract: Commonplace in medical, financial, legal, regulatory and managerial settings are surrogates who make decisions for others. In this paper's experiment, third party Choosers allocate $10 between a proximate Friend and a more distant Receiver. Choosers respond to indicated Friend preferences and defaults that stipulate a baseline allocation that is either equal or unequal (Friend favoring). I _nd that Friends (expressing preferences) and Choosers (selecting allocations) favor defaults, while Choosers predominantly follow their Friends' preferences. Combining e_ects, an equal (v. unequal) default produces a 25 percent increase in equal allocations. Potential implications for organ donation are discussed.

title: Occlusion-Aware Visual Object Tracking with SAM2-Based Segmentation via Temporal Convolutional Networks and a Dual-Memory Bank
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Occlusion-Aware Visual Object Tracking with SAM2-Based Segmentation via Temporal Convolutional Networks and a Dual-Memory Bank
detail.abstract: Visual Object Tracking (VOT) remains challenging under occlusion scenarios, where traditional trackers often suffer from feature degradation and target loss. To address this issue, we propose OASAMT, an occlusion-aware tracking framework that equips SAM2 with explicit temporal occlusion reasoning via two Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) and a Dual-Memory Bank (DMB). Specifically, two TCN-based modules are designed to model temporal occlusion dynamics: the Temporal Occlusion Classifier (TOC) for inferring target occlusion states using confidence scores, mask IoU, and area ratio; and the Temporal Occlusion Predictor (TOP) for forecasting target bounding boxes during occlusion. The proposed DMB consists of a Non-Occlusion Memory Bank (N-OMB) and an Occlusion Memory Bank (OMB), explicitly decoupling reliable and occluded representations to prevent memory contamination and improve re-detection after occlusion. Additionally, to facilitate systematic evaluation under occlusion scenarios, we construct OccTrack, a dedicated occlusion-oriented dataset derived from four UAV-view benchmarks. Extensive experiments were conducted on the OccTrack, LaSOT, LaSOText, and GOT-10k datasets. The results demonstrate that OASAMT consistently outperforms SAM2.1 and other advanced trackers in both occlusion-specific and general tracking scenarios. The code and dataset will be made available.

title: Value Fluid Dynamics: A Proposal for a "Double Parallel Circuit" Economic Model in the Post-Singularity Era
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Value Fluid Dynamics: A Proposal for a "Double Parallel Circuit" Economic Model in the Post-Singularity Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests

detail.abstract: This paper presents an economic theory explicitly designed for the "Post-Singularity" future, where AI surpasses human intelligence and traditional scarcity is resolved. With the advancement of AI and automation, the traditional "Labor Theory of Value" is collapsing. This paper proposes a new economic framework, "Value Fluid Dynamics," which applies the laws of physics (thermodynamics and circuitry) to macroeconomics. The author argues that modern poverty stems from connecting "survival" and "labor" in series. By reconfiguring these into a "Parallel Circuit," where Basic Income functions as a superconducting bypass (R \approx 0) and labor functions as a filament loop (R > 0), we can achieve a steady-state economy. Furthermore, this paper introduces the concept of "Initial Human Asset," calculating that every citizen possesses an inherent asset value of 200 million yen based on Japan's GNI.

title: Regulating Sports Prediction Markets
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Business Law,  and City University of New York - Baruch College, Zicklin School of Business

detail.title: Regulating Sports Prediction Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming __ University of Illinois Law Review __

detail.abstract:
Prediction market companies such as Kalshi and Polymarket have recently burst onto the scene and begun selling contracts that allow buyers to predict the outcome of events such as sports games and political elections. By structuring these contracts as financial instruments, prediction market companies seek to overturn the traditional regulatory framework for sports betting. Instead of being supervised by state gaming commissions, prediction contracts on sports events would be federally regulated as “swaps” under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Such a jurisdictional leap intentionally carries dramatic implications for how sports gaming contracts are taxed and licensed, and for what consumer protection rules are in place with respect to the end-users, sports bettors.

This article presents an early analysis of this emerging phenomenon, which represents one of the most ambitious attempts at regulatory arbitrage in recent memory for any industry. In doing so, it clarifies issues that will be critical for evaluating the appropriate regulatory framework going forward. These include: (a) a comparison of the sports gaming industry with prediction markets (b) the comparative advantages of state gaming commissions versus federal regulators at the CFTC; and (c) an overview of the current caselaw, which has been thrown into uncertainty by a growing federal court split.
Ultimately, this article suggests a cautious approach that allows room for concurrent state and federal regulation of sports prediction contracts, at least initially. By allowing a temporary phase of jurisdictional competition, state and federal regulators will be incentivized to provide credible solutions to the novel problems posed by sports prediction contracts. Policymakers will also have time to gather empirical data on the relative performance of each regulatory structure.

title: Life’s Big Decisions in the Age of AI
affiliations: UCLA Anderson, New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Life’s Big Decisions in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: The Big Decisions in our lives, having a child, getting married, getting educated, etc. are transformative decisions that are hard to make. As a result, people often seek advice before making them. However, since people tend to live in homophilous social networks the advice received from their friends and neighbors may simply reinforce the decisions that people like them are already making. We investigate whether the advice offered by ChatGPT for such decisions can be useful in broadening the advice people receive and how such advice varies as we change the prompted socioeconomic backgrounds of the advisee and advisor. We find that advice tends to be confirmatory for low-income groups, in that it reinforces their established choices, while being dis-confirming for high-income groups, where it prompts reconsideration. Furthermore, even when suggesting the same choice, ChatGPT justifies that choice differently depending on who it is talking to. These findings suggest that AI-generated advice may differentially shape life’s Big Decisions across social strata.

title: Financial Development, Credit Rationing and Informal Credit Markets: Implications for Pattern of Trade
affiliations: Lal Bahadur Shastri Institute of Management and

detail.title: Financial Development, Credit Rationing and Informal Credit Markets: Implications for Pattern of Trade
detail.abstract: Firms differ in the extent to which they get access to formal and informal credit sources in developing economies. In developing economies, banks ration credit due to higher perceived borrower risk, information asymmetry, lack of collateral, and market inefficiencies. Due to financial constraints in formal credit markets, firms often seek alternative funding from informal sources such as friends, family, and moneylenders, even though it comes at a higher borrowing cost. Financial development can help expand access to credit by reducing structural barriers and mitigating the effects of credit rationing. To analyze these dynamics, our paper developed a theoretical model that examines the relationships among credit rationing, financial development, and informal credit markets, and their impact on trade patterns. Financial capital is introduced into the standard workhorse of trade theory, i.e., Dixit-Stiglitz-Krugman (DSK) model of international trade under monopolistic competition. We showed that financial development does not affect trade and production outcomes when firms have access only to formal credit markets, whereas when firms gain access to informal credit markets alongside credit rationing, it increases the number of varieties produced but at the cost of lower output per variety. However, the higher the interest gap between the formal and informal credit markets, the higher will be the marginal impact of the degree of financial development on the pattern of trade. We have also conducted a small empirical motivational exercise to support our findings from theoretical model.

title: The Unintended Costs of Early Retirement Policies: Evidence from Italy’s Quota 100 Reform
affiliations: and University of Bergamo

detail.title: The Unintended Costs of Early Retirement Policies: Evidence from Italy’s Quota 100 Reform
detail.abstract: This paper examines the unintended consequences of policies perceived as inequitable by leveraging Italy’s Quota 100 pension reform, which denied early retirement to workers with identical contribution histories who did not meet an age cutoff. Using SHARE data and a difference-in-differences design, we first establish that excluded workers experienced no change in unemployment or disability status, while their relative probability of being retired fell mechanically. We then document a significant deterioration in their mental health, with effects emerging immediately upon the reform’s introduction and persisting for at least two years. These effects are concentrated among workers who satisfy the contribution requirement but are denied eligibility solely on the basis of age, implicating perceived unfairness as a primary channel. Using European Social Survey data and a regression discontinuity design, we find that the reform led to a reduction in trust in institutions among age-ineligible workers. Finally, electoral data show that the League, the reform’s principal architect, suffered vote share losses in municipalities with higher concentrations of excluded workers, with penaltiesexceeding any gains accrued in areas with more beneficiaries.

title: Reforming the Civil Service: Impacts on Engagement, Job Satisfaction, Burnout, and Turnover Intentions
affiliations: The George Washington University and

detail.title: Reforming the Civil Service: Impacts on Engagement, Job Satisfaction, Burnout, and Turnover Intentions
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the causal impact of the 2025 U.S. federal personnel reforms on employment, employee engagement, job satisfaction, burnout, job search behavior, and perceptions about their workplace. Using administrative and survey data, we implement a differencein-differences design comparing federal employees to observationally similar state-and local government employees before and after the reforms. Event-study estimates show near-parallel pre-trends (2022-2024) and a sharp post-reform divergence in 2025. Baseline estimates indicate a meaningful decline in federal employment and employee engagement relative to the state control group, accompanied by reductions in job satisfaction and corresponding increases in reported burnout and job search activity. Heterogeneity analyses show that these effects are driven almost entirely by federal workers who identify as Democrats, and to some extent Independents, with little to no impact on their Republican colleagues. We also find that perceptions of workplace practices, like trust in leadership, play a moderating role.

title: Economic Exposure and Climate Policy Support
affiliations: Utrecht University, Utrecht University and Utrecht University

detail.title: Economic Exposure and Climate Policy Support
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the relationship between economic exposure to climate policies and climate policy support. We develop a stylised theoretical model to decompose exposure through income, energy spending and vehicle use, and define consistent measures of these exposure channels. We then combine detailed Dutch household administrative data and survey data on climate policy support and find that higher exposure is robustly associated with lower support for stronger climate policies across all three channels. Further analysis reveals that high electricity rather than high natural gas spending is associated with reduced support, and vehicle fuel efficiency is a more important predictor of support than income-adjusted kilometres driven. Income exposure, proxied by the sectoral carbon-intensity of jobs, is particularly salient among older and lower–to-middle educated respondents.

title: Co-Benefits of Substance Abuse Regulation on Temperature and Violent Crime
affiliations: Ifo Institute and

detail.title: Co-Benefits of Substance Abuse Regulation on Temperature and Violent Crime
detail.abstract: Higher temperatures can increase substance abuse and exacerbate its physiological effects on the human body, raising the risk of violent behavior. Using administrative crime records and daily temperatures in the United States between 1991 and 2023, we show that two public policies regulating substance abuse — the expansion of substance abuse treatment facilities and the reformulation of the prescription opioid OxyContin — substantially moderate the impact of temperature on interpersonal violent crime. We monetize the policy benefits for intimate partner violence, the most widespread crime in the United States, and show that substance abuse regulations can be a cost-effective tool for climate adaptation.

title: The Hidden Objectivism of Revealed-Preference Welfare Economics
affiliations: University of St. Gallen - Institute of Economy and the Environment (IWOe-HSG)

detail.title: The Hidden Objectivism of Revealed-Preference Welfare Economics
detail.abstract: Revealed preference theory (RPT) and its behavioral extension (BRPT) underpin an important strand of welfare economics. Their normative appeal rests on the claim that welfare can be inferred from observed behavior without substantive assumptions about what agents should value - a property I call value neutrality. This paper argues that such neutrality is structurally impossible. I develop a framework - the triangulation problem - identifying five dimensions along which inference from behavior to welfare is underdetermined: the partitioning of the alternative space, the preference domain, the choice rule, the social technology, and the phenomenological mapping from preferences to experience. A sixth problem - the agent's lack of experiential acquaintance with novel alternatives - compounds the underdeterminacy. Resolving these dimensions requires substantive commitments about value rationality - about what agents ought to care about and what counts for welfare. No specification of (B)RPT is both determinate enough to yield welfare rankings and neutral with respect to value rationality. I show that this impossibility entails a collapse thesis: (B)RPT understands itself as a subjectivist theory of well-being, but every operational specification embeds objectivist commitments - attitude-independent claims about what is basically good for the agent - in its auxiliary assumptions. In normative use, (B)RPT is a de-facto objectivist theory that presents itself in subjectivist form, concealing commitments that require philosophical justification behind an appearance of empirical neutrality.

title: The Content Moderator's Dilemma: Removal of Toxic Content and Distortions to Online Discourse
affiliations: Bocconi, Bocconi University and Bocconi University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Content Moderator's Dilemma: Removal of Toxic Content and Distortions to Online Discourse
detail.abstract: There is an ongoing debate about how to moderate toxic speech on social media and the impact of content moderation on online discourse. This paper proposes and validates a methodology for measuring the content-moderation-induced distortions in online discourse using text embeddings from computational linguistics. Applying the method to a representative sample of 5 million US political Tweets, we find that removing toxic Tweets significantly alters the semantic composition of content. The magnitudes of the distortions are comparable to removing 4 out of 67 topics from the online discourse at random. This finding is consistent across different embedding models, toxicity metrics, and samples. Importantly, we demonstrate that these effects are not solely driven by toxic language but by the removal of topics often expressed in toxic form. We propose an alternative approach to content moderation that uses generative Large Language Models to rephrase toxic Tweets, preserving their salvageable content rather than removing them entirely. We show that this rephrasing strategy reduces toxicity while mitigating distortions in online content.

title: How Does Administrative-market Synergy Drive Green Breakthrough Innovation? Empirical Evidence from Generalized Random Forests
affiliations: Guangdong University of Finance, Guangdong University of Finance, Guangdong University of Finance, Guangdong University of Finance and Guangdong University of Finance

detail.title: How Does Administrative-market Synergy Drive Green Breakthrough Innovation? Empirical Evidence from Generalized Random Forests
detail.abstract: Based on evidence from Chinese listed companies from 2009 to 2022, this study finds that the synergy between the Low-Carbon City Pilot Policy (LCCPP) and the Carbon Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) exerts a significant positive impact on corporate green breakthrough innovation (GBI). This conclusion remains robust across a series of tests. Mechanism analysis reveals that the synergistic policy fosters GBI primarily by cultivating stable patient capital, accelerating digital technology application, agglomerating human capital, and enhancing media attention. Furthermore, the heterogeneity analysis using generalized random forest (GRF) discovers that the policy effect surges rapidly once the largest shareholder’s ownership percentage (TOP1) exceeds 0.5, displays an inverted U-shaped relationship with the asset-liability ratio (LEV), and shows a positive correlation with the book-to-market ratio (BM). Further analysis indicates that the synergistic policy intervention generates a markedly larger effect than either single policy, while the chronological order of implementation shows no significant impact. These results offer important implications for policymakers. Policy synergy can promote GBI, and tailored supporting measures based on firm characteristics can improve implementation efficiency.

title: Political Dynasties and the Future of Public Administration in the Philippines
affiliations: Public Administration and Political Science, Don Mariano Marcos Memorial State University

detail.title: Political Dynasties and the Future of Public Administration in the Philippines
detail.abstract: Political dynasties remain a pervasive feature of the Philippine political landscape, shaping governance structures, public resource allocation, and institutional accountability. This article critically examines how dynastic politics influences the practice and reform of public administration in the Philippines. By synthesizing multidisciplinary literature from political science, public administration, and development studies, the paper argues that reducing dynastic influence requires institutional reform, citizen empowerment, and strengthened administrative meritocracy. The persistence of political families presents both challenges and opportunities for advancing a more accountable, professional, and development-oriented public administration system.

title: The Value of Information: A Puzzle
affiliations: and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: The Value of Information: A Puzzle
detail.abstract: We show that under mild assumptions, the total value of information to informed traders in the market can be measured by the covariance between price changes and order flow. This covariance captures noise trader losses, which equal informed trader gains when market making is competitive. We estimate the value of information using high frequency data on US equities at about $3.5 million per year for the average stock. The aggregate value of information is about 0.04% of market cap, which is considerably lower than the 0.67% in fees investors pay each year searching for superior returns (French 2008). We discuss potential resolutions for these puzzling findings.

title: Border Order and Identity Density in the Middle East: A Realist-Constructivist Analysis

detail.title: Border Order and Identity Density in the Middle East: A Realist-Constructivist Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: zip
declarations.ethicsApproval: Unethical and Onesided.
declarations.funderStatement: zip

detail.abstract: Borders in the Middle East exhibit varying degrees of stability, ranging from frozen conflicts to episodic violent flare-ups. Traditional accounts attribute instability to colonial legacies, power asymmetries, or ideological rivalry, but these frameworks provide only partial explanatory power. This study develops a synthetic realist-constructivist model, arguing that border outcomes are determined by the interplay of territorial contestation, identity density, and normative enforcement mechanisms. Focusing on five major regional powers-Iran, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Israel-the analysis examines how internal identity diversity interacts with border dynamics, influencing both the potential for conflict and the efficacy of enforcement. Through detailed case studies, including Iran-Iraq, Turkey-Syria, Israel-Lebanon, and Saudi-Yemen frontiers, the paper demonstrates that high identity density without robust enforcement produces volatility, whereas strong enforcement mechanisms can stabilize even identity-sensitive borders. The findings carry significant implications for European Union policy and international efforts to manage border disputes in the region.

title: Public Infrastructure Provision, Residents' Preference and Willingness to Live: Evidence from Kaduna Metropolis, Nigeria
affiliations: Nuhu Bamalli Polytechnic and Nuhu Bamalli Polytechnic

detail.title: Public Infrastructure Provision, Residents' Preference and Willingness to Live: Evidence from Kaduna Metropolis, Nigeria
detail.abstract: The growing concern about the non-provision of public infrastructural facilities in accordance to residents' preference in most developing countries and the recognition that people choose to live in an area with their preferred infrastructure provision necessitates this study. Therefore, this study assessed the effects of public infrastructural provision and resident's preference on willingness to reside in Kaduna metropolis, with a view to proposing areas of improvement. the objectives of this study are to assess the level of public infrastructure provision, to assess the level of residents' preference with public infrastructural provision, to assess the level of residents' satisfaction with public infrastructure provision, to assess the level of residents' willingness to live and to determine the effects of public infrastructural provision and residents' preference on willingness to live in the study area. The study adopted a quantitative approach, where data was collected using questionnaires from 382 household head randomly selected from the study area. The instrument validity was established through scrutiny and evaluation by the research supervisor and two experts in the study area, and reliability was determined via Cronbach's alpha coefficient reliability test. The data collected was subjected to descriptive and inferential statistics to examine the degree of agreement and significance of the various variables. The study revealed that 99.3 percent of willingness to live is influenced by infrastructure provision and residents' preference. Both infrastructure provision and residents' preference have a positive and significant effect on residence willing to live. It is recommended that public infrastructural facilities provision in the area should be based on the resident's preference and need, and there is need for effective policy implementation to address the problems of inadequate infrastructural facilities provision.

title: Fiscal Limits to Protectionism: The 2025 U.S. Tariff Laffer Curve
affiliations: McMaster University and Georgetown University, School of Foreign Service in Qatar

detail.title: Fiscal Limits to Protectionism: The 2025 U.S. Tariff Laffer Curve
detail.abstract: We quantify the Tariff Laffer Curve for the U.S. using a multi-sector Ricardian model calibrated to the 2025 US trade war. We find revenue-maximizing tariffs of 20–30 percent and welfare-maximizing rates of 0–10 percent. We define the Marginal Fiscal Efficiency Index to partition tariffs into welfare-improving, trade-off, and revenue-decreasing regions. Expanding the trade war to more partners raises peak revenue even under retaliation, whereas coordinated retaliation sharply erodes welfare. By January 2026, 20 percent of U.S. tariffs exceed their Laffer peaks. Inverse-optimum estimation reveals diminished U.S. concern for foreign welfare, punitive treatment of China, and rising revenue motives.

title: Uncertainty about Legal Status and the Economic and Social Integration of Refugees
affiliations: , VATT Institute for Economic Research and VATT Institute for Economic Research

detail.title: Uncertainty about Legal Status and the Economic and Social Integration of Refugees
detail.abstract: Refugees spend months or even years waiting for asylum decisions under uncertainty. To study how this waiting time influences their economic and social integration into the host country, we use information on the universe of asylum seekers to Finland and follow their trajectories with comprehensive administrative records. We leverage variation in processing times that are due to quasi-random allocation of cases to immigration caseworkers who handle applications at different speeds. We find that longer waiting times delay entry into labor markets, reduce skill investments and create costs to host country public finances. However, longer waiting times also reduce the likelihood of committing crimes and increase turnout in local elections. This suggests that the language and integration courses accessed during the waiting time can help entrench an understanding or appreciation of local norms and rules. For underage asylum seekers, we find no negative impacts on educational outcomes, crime or political participation, likely because all children are granted access to a stable environment with comprehensive education and other integration services regardless of their legal status.

title: The Great Detour and the Need for Macroeconomic Theory
affiliations: University of Massachusetts at Amherst - College of Social and Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Great Detour and the Need for Macroeconomic Theory
detail.abstract: This paper makes three points. First, big data, advanced econometrics and sophisticated computational techniques do not obviate the need for macroeconomic theory and small, analytical models. The design and interpretation of empirical studies and large-scale models are guided by economic theory. Second, the current macroeconomic theory employs simplistic microeconomic assumptions with little empirical support, imposes heroic restrictions on interaction structures and agent heterogeneity, and applies the same models to economies with widely di¤erent structures and institutions. Third, a more fruitful structuralist and behavioral approach builds on empirical evidence of systematic, macroeconomically relevant behavioral patterns, recognizes the e¤ects of structural and institutional factors, and places the interaction across sectors and between di¤erent types of decision makers at the center of the analysis.

title: Antitrust Law's Breakup Obsession
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School

detail.title: Antitrust Law's Breakup Obsession
detail.abstract:
Antitrust actions against dominant firms, particularly in big tech, have led to vociferous calls for “break up” remedies.  The federal antitrust enforcement Agencies routinely request structural remedies as well, and have done so since the early history of antitrust law.  In contrast, the antitrust statutes make clear that the preferred remedy for antitrust violations is not a breakup but rather an injunction.  After an initial period of acquiescence in government requests for breakup remedies, courts came to follow the statutes and frequently reject government breakup requests.

The Supreme Court requires that an antitrust remedy “restore competitive conditions.” An effective remedy moves the dominated market toward lower prices, higher output, and removes unreasonable restraints on innovation. Under that standard, breakup remedies in monopolization cases almost never succeed. The core problem is design: courts are poorly equipped to re-engineer firms into competitive market structures, especially when dealing with highly integrated production systems, networks, or digital architectures.  Most court ordered breakups in monopolization cases do not break up the monopoly at all, but rather spin off a complementary product.  Others replace national monopolies with regional monopolies, but with no impact on pricing or output. Yet others require dominant firms to create new competitors, which almost always fail, or impose costly interconnection or other sharing agreements.

The problem is even more severe in digital markets such as Google Search or Facebook.  Three features of digital products strongly favor non-breakup remedies.  First, digital assets can almost never be split into multiple pieces without destroying their functionality.  Second, however, digital assets can be shared much more readily than traditional tactile assets.  Third, one characteristic of digital assets is that rivals can increase their own output quickly and at low marginal cost.  As a result, an injunction that removes provisions that exclude or disfavor rivals or that impose nonexclusive licensing can generate prompt rival expansion.  Indeed, the most underrated of remedies in those areas where it can be used is the non-exclusive license, which comes much closer than any breakup to creating head-to-head competition among multiple firms.

Nevertheless, nonexclusive licensing cannot go so far that it turns competitors into mere sales agents of the dominant firm.  As the district court recognized in the Google (search) decision, a remedy must contemplate both competition and product differentiation by rivals who are committed not only to selling the product but also to developing their own infrastructure.  An effective remedy improves market performance rather than creating more or smaller firms for their own sake.

title: The Millennials Moving Beyond Regenerative Governance Level: All GNH Nationals Engineer the Sufficiency Sustainable Freedom State Skills Self-Sufficiency and Ecological Stability
affiliations: Swiss School Of Business and Management

detail.title: The Millennials Moving Beyond Regenerative Governance Level: All GNH Nationals Engineer the Sufficiency Sustainable Freedom State Skills Self-Sufficiency and Ecological Stability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract:
Operational Sovereignty The discourse surrounding national security, sustainability, and economic development frequently misinterprets the concept of self-sufficiency. In contemporary geopolitical analysis, self-sufficiency is often erroneously conflated with isolationism, protectionism, or anachronistic autarky. In reality, self-sufficiency represents a higher maturity stage of governance. If a systemic architecture can feed, heal, educate, empower, and protect its people without collapsing under the pressure of exogenous shocks—whether those shocks manifest as global pandemics, supply chain ruptures, or climate-induced disasters—that constitutes governance competence at the highest conceivable tier. 
This level of competence is not achieved through declarative policy or international compliance reporting. It is achieved through operational sovereignty, which demands the rigorous application of integrated systems engineering, decentralized infrastructure design, and closed-loop resource circularity. To structure this evolution properly, governance must be analyzed through a reality-based maturity continuum that measures a state’s capacity to absorb shocks and sustain its population autonomously.
This investigates the structural, ecological, and socio-economic frameworks of ancient and indigenous civilizations to extract actionable mechanisms for long-term agrarian self-sufficiency. Contrasting the modern industrial paradigm—which prioritizes perpetual gross domestic product (GDP) growth—with historical models optimized for socio-ecological equilibrium, this analysis evaluates seven long-lasting systems: Ancient Egypt, the Indus Valley, Dynastic China, the Andean civilizations, traditional Japanese Satoyama, Indigenous Australian land management, and the Ethiopian Highlands. The historical data demonstrates that while modern linear economies struggle to meet short-term sustainable development goals, multi-millennial resilience is achievable. The findings indicate that true sustainability relies on decentralized food production, localized water security, robust organic circular economies, and a cultural or educational apparatus that strictly aligns human resource extraction with the regenerative carrying capacity of the local biosphere.

title: Quantitative Evaluation of Soil Pore Alterations under Machinery Traffic using Micro-CT Imaging: A Case Study in Sugarcane Fields
affiliations: Shahid Chamran University of Ahvaz, Shahid Chamran University of Ahvaz, Aarhus University and Aarhus University

detail.title: Quantitative Evaluation of Soil Pore Alterations under Machinery Traffic using Micro-CT Imaging: A Case Study in Sugarcane Fields
detail.abstract: Machinery-induced soil compaction during sugarcane harvesting is a major driver of soil structural degradation, yet its pore-scale effects remain insufficiently quantified. Here, X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) was used to quantify pore structure changes in soils sampled from the 0–6 cm layer under undisturbed conditions (BH) and after harvesting traffic at 75% (AH-75%) and 100% (AH-100%) wagon load capacities. Compared with BH, compaction increased pore number by >110% while reducing average pore size by 56–61%, indicating extensive aggregate fragmentation and loss of large functional pores. Circularity and solidity increased by up to 18% and 22%, respectively, reflecting simplified and denser pore geometry. Three-dimensional analyses showed substantial reductions in macropore volume (−35 to −48%), mean diameter (−28 to −41%), and connectivity (−40 to −55%), with the strongest effects in the surface 0–3 cm layer. Depth-wise analyses further revealed reduced average porosity and homogenized pore distribution under compacted conditions. Notably, AH-75% exhibited greater losses in macropore continuity and connectivity than AH-100%, despite lower applied loads, highlighting the non-linear response of soil structure to traffic intensity and the critical influence of soil moisture. Overall, compaction shifted the pore system from a connected, macropore-dominated architecture to a fragmented and hydrologically restrictive structure, impairing water infiltration, gas diffusion, and root penetration. These findings emphasize the need for controlled traffic management in sugarcane systems and demonstrate micro-CT as a robust, non-destructive tool for quantifying soil structural degradation beyond conventional bulk density-based assessments.

title: Distributional Learning for Tail Risk: Optimal Transport, Coherent Risk, and Financial Applications

detail.title: Distributional Learning for Tail Risk: Optimal Transport, Coherent Risk, and Financial Applications
detail.abstract: Modern financial decision-making is dominated by tail risk rather than conditional expectations. This paper develops a unified framework for distributional learning in financial settings by combining optimal transport geometry, coherent risk theory, and statistical learning. We model predictive systems as operators that map observable features to conditional probability laws and study how nonlinear risk functionals act on these learned distributions. Building on the spectral representation of coherent risk measures and their dual formulations, we establish stability results showing that Expected Shortfall and related tail-sensitive risk measures are Lipschitz continuous in Wasserstein space. These bounds provide a direct link between distributional learning accuracy and robustness of tail-risk estimates. The analysis further connects distributional learning with distributionally robust optimization, interpreting learned distributions as centers of ambiguity sets defined by optimal transport metrics. Finitesample guarantees are derived by combining Wasserstein convergence rates with stability of coherent risk operators, yielding explicit bounds on tail-risk estimation error. We discuss implications across trading, credit, and XVA applications, and interpret the results in the context of modern regulatory frameworks emphasizing tail stability and model robustness. Overall, the paper positions distributional learning as a natural paradigm for financial risk modeling in environments where tail events and distributional shifts are primary drivers of decision-making.

title: Power in the Pitch: Narratives and Market Value of Solar PV Homes in New Zealand
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Power in the Pitch: Narratives and Market Value of Solar PV Homes in New Zealand

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by a Marsden Fast-Start grant MFP-NIW2202 from the Royal Society of New Zealand Te Apārangi.

detail.abstract: Residential solar photovoltaics have expanded rapidly in many countries, yet little is known about how solar features are communicated in property marketing or how they are capitalised in housing markets with low incentives and limited uptake. Existing international research primarily focuses on price effects in higher-penetration settings and has not included large-scale analysis of listing narratives. This study addresses these gaps by examining how solar homes are described in real estate advertising and whether solar installations influence sale prices and days on market in Aotearoa New Zealand. The analysis uses a 4-year panel of 79,944 matched listings and sales, combining nearest-neighbour propensity score matching, fixed-effects regression and topic modelling of listing descriptions. Results show that solar homes are marketed through lifestyle, rural and quality cues rather than explicit sustainability framing, suggesting that PV is bundled with broader amenity signals rather than positioned as a distinct attribute. PV-equipped homes command an average sale price premium of 1.34 per cent, with no significant difference in days on market. Effects do not vary with solar irradiance or local solar penetration, indicating limited salience of site-specific energy benefits in buyer decisionmaking. The study contributes theoretically by integrating price capitalisation, behavioural economics and marketing narratives. It offers an explanation for why sustainability framing may be limited in a setting where financial incentives are weak. Practically, the findings highlight a need for clearer communication of PV performance and financial benefits in real estate markets, along with policy measures that strengthen the salience for prospective buyers.

title: What Counts as Corruption? Alternative Indicators for SDG16.5 in the Era of AI
affiliations: The University of Sydney Law School

detail.title: What Counts as Corruption? Alternative Indicators for SDG16.5 in the Era of AI

declarations.funderStatement: Part of this research was funded by the Australian Research Council through grants CE200100005 and IE240100096

detail.abstract: The inclusion of anticorruption objectives among the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) must be celebrated. As then-Secretary-General Kofi Annan noted to the General Assembly in 1998, good governance could be "the single most important factor in eradicating poverty and promoting development". Target 16.5, "Substantially reduce corruption and bribery in all their forms" materialises this objective within the SDGs, setting an vision of a (substantially) less corrupt world by 2030. However, as explored in this chapter, the quantification aspect of this target and its indicators, risk reinforcing stereotypes that see corruption as a global South (or "majority world") issue and primes policymakers and other stakeholders to see all corruption through the bribery prism. The measurements to assess success in substantially reducing corruption and bribery in all their forms are two indicators tracking the proportion of persons (16.5.1) or businesses (16.5.2) who have paid (or were asked for) a bribe to a public official during the previous 12 months (Statistical Commission 2017, 30/71). This chapter focuses concretely on these indicators and contends that they are not adequate to assess changes in the incidence of corruption across countries. First, they use bribery as a proxy for corruption, introducing a metonymic approach that is not representative of the corruption reality in many countries. Second, the approach quantifies bribery based exclusively on the persons' and firms' direct experiences in their relations with public officials, introducing severe methodological limitations. Third, it builds into the indicators an intrinsic bias against global South countries. Bribes are unequivocally a much more common instance of corruption in everyday life in countries with lower per capita incomes. If we looked for corruption beyond bribery, the picture could be different. For example, there is some evidence that the incidence of favouritism may not be that dissimilar in developing and developed countries. Measuring those instances would better complement the bribery indicators. This chapter encourages us to consider a different quantification system based on big data analysis, which could be fairer, and easier to assess over the 15-year span of the SDGs. This could be possible with the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). AI can be used to track the evolution of countries over time in a comparable manner. This makes the creation of a third indicator advisable and feasible. The chapter presents two possible candidates for that third indicator around procurement data and health-related payments. These measurements could be the basis of other complementary indicators in the final years of the SDGs or, more likely, a springboard towards a more responsive measurement of anticorruption progress post-2030.

title: Belonging Mismatch and Integrated Development of Urban Agglomerations and Inter-Group City Based on Network Community Division, Evidence from China
affiliations: Guizhou University of Finance and Economics and Guizhou University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Belonging Mismatch and Integrated Development of Urban Agglomerations and Inter-Group City Based on Network Community Division, Evidence from China
detail.abstract: The integration of urban agglomerations has a profound impact on the high-quality economic development of China, and the problem of belonging mismatch of cities within, outside and between urban agglomerations in China has become the most critical factor affecting and restricting the integrated development in recent years. Therefore, this paper takes the 19 approved and pending approved urban agglomerations as the research objects, and constructs the inter-city economic correlation networks in four different years, and conducts the research on the evolution of network characteristics, community division and urban agglomeration belonging mismatch of China. The study finds that the following three types of belonging mismatch exist in the process of integrated development of urban agglomerations in China: first, cities within urban agglomerations are not well integrated with other cities; second, cities outside the scope of urban agglomerations are strongly related to the corresponding urban agglomerations but are not included in the plan of urban agglomerations; third, cities located between multiple urban agglomerations are not clearly identified in the planning and actual development. The integrated development of urban agglomerations is proposed from the aspects of breaking administrative boundaries, coordinated urban development, improving transportation infrastructure and environmental governance.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Legal Reasoning: A Practical Framework for Ethical AI Implementation in Legal Practice Kentucky's Local Counsel as a Case Study in Hallucination-Resistant Legal AI
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Neuro-Symbolic Legal Reasoning: A Practical Framework for Ethical AI Implementation in Legal Practice Kentucky's Local Counsel as a Case Study in Hallucination-Resistant Legal AI
detail.abstract: The integration of symbolic reasoning with neural methods-termed neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence-offers transformative potential for legal technology by combining the interpretability and logical rigor of knowledge graphs with the generative fluency of large language models (LLMs). This paper presents Kentucky's Local Counsel, an advanced neuro-evaluated against the Stanford Legal Fictions framework (n = 2,989), 92.2% accuracy on a Kentucky-adapted LegalBench framework, and 85.3% on KY-PRBench-a fifty-question professional reasoning benchmark on which KLC outperformed the highest-scoring frontier model by 14.9 percentage points with a 99.6% citation grounding rate against frontier models' 52-58%. The evaluation also documents a methodologically significant finding: the automated LLM judge hallucinated legal premises on approximately one-third of scored responses, systematically underscoring the knowledge-grounded system. The paper compares the approach to commercial alternatives, addresses the scaling hypothesis for professional legal reasoning, and discusses implications for responsible AI deployment in accordance with professional responsibility obligations.

title: The Missing Inflation Loop: Why High Income No Longer Means High Living Standards

detail.title: The Missing Inflation Loop: Why High Income No Longer Means High Living Standards
detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural explanation for the growing divergence between measured real income and lived economic experience. While conventional inflation adjustments remove nominal price changes within a given consumption basket, they implicitly assume stability in the set of non-discretionary goods and services required for effective economic participation. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile in structurally complex economies. The paper introduces the concept of basket-expansion inflation, defined as the structural enlargement of the non-discretionary consumption bundle independently of price movements within that bundle. As technological integration deepens, housing constraints intensify, and institutional complexity increases, a rising share of income is allocated toward maintaining economic inclusion rather than expanding discretionary welfare. This framework helps explain why sustained increases in real GDP per capita may coexist with stagnant perceptions of living standards and offers a structural reinterpretation of the Easterlin Paradox. Rather than attributing the divergence between income growth and wellbeing solely to psychological adaptation or relative comparison, the paper argues that part of measured growth compensates for rising participation costs not captured by conventional price indices. The contribution is conceptual rather than normative. It does not challenge national accounting methodology but refines the interpretation of long-run income dynamics by distinguishing between growth that expands discretionary choice and growth that sustains position within an evolving participation structure.
