title: Land Use Policy

detail.title: Land Use Policy
detail.abstract: The dispossession of people from their land was a primary aspect of the war in Colombia. As an important part of the peace negotiations and current efforts at peace-building, land restitution in the country is a large-scale, multifaceted effort intended to address one of the more difficult components of the peace process. While there are many important features to the Colombian land restitution process, six stand out as particularly valuable, and therefore important for the international community to study for applicability elsewhere. These include, 1) involvement of affected communities in the derivation of the restitution program; 2) the construction of a database of land dispossession in the country; 3) the inclusion of gender considerations in the legal foundation for restitution; 4) constitutional protections for Afro-Colombian communities and indigenous peoples who are due restitution; 5) beginning the restitution process while the conflict is still underway; and 6) managing informality in land rights.

title: Machine Learning Modelling of the Impact of Socio-Economic Transition on GHG Emissions in East Africa
affiliations: Makerere University, Makerere University and Makerere University

detail.title: Machine Learning Modelling of the Impact of Socio-Economic Transition on GHG Emissions in East Africa
detail.abstract: This research sheds light on the modelled forecast of Greenhouse gas emission pathways across East Africa, by highlighting the roles played by urbanization, energy usage and growing income. The research engaged a balanced panel of five East African countries; Burundi, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and Uganda over a thirty year period from 1993 to 2022 using secondary data harvested from EU’s EDGAR emission data synchronized with demographic and energy indicators from World bank’s WDI data. The study compared the findings of benchmark econometric models; fixed-random effects, and error - correction against machine learning strategies which comprised of Random Forests, LSTM neural networks and Gradient boosting methods to evaluate the forecasting performance and identify the dominant predictors. The study result revealed that urbanization consistently raises emissions, moreover per capita GDP mainly influences Greenhouse gas emissions through cross-country than in-country dynamics. Further revealed was that per capita Energy use was the strongest forward looking predictor, more-so while Traditional panel regressions offer limited predictive accuracy; machine learning models had tremendous performance, also: the LSTM reduces out-of-sample RMSE by more than 30 percent relative to fixed effects. On further analysis Scenario forecasts to 2040 results showed that baseline trend is associated with steady rise in emissions, however on the other hand an energy transition trajectory substantially flattens emission growth. The findings of this research underscore the importance of comparing econometric and machine learning strategies for shaping climate policies in developing economies. As the East African block is climbing the stairs of development; the trajectory depends on adequate management of the rapid urbanization and adoption of sustainable energy sources, this transition offers diverse opportunities that can be explored as mitigation measures under the East African Community (EAC) framework. The study is therefore imperative as it serves as a traficator to give warning signs to ensire the East African Community which is on a fast growwing trajectory does not get locked in an emission intensive growth and therefore provide guidance to policy makers to shape and decouple the economy from an emission intensive economic trap.

title: Impact of Institutional Quality on Stock Market Performance in Emerging Economies
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria, Nile University of Nigeria and Nile University of Nigeria

detail.title: Impact of Institutional Quality on Stock Market Performance in Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: Weak governance structures and fragile legal systems continue to undermine investor confidence and financial market development in many emerging economies, motivating an examination of how institutional quality shapes stock market performance. This study investigates the relationship for the period 2000–2024 using dynamic panel estimation based on the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM). Key governance indicators—control of corruption, government effectiveness, political stability, regulatory quality, rule of law, and voice and accountability—are employed to explain variations in stock market performance measured by market capitalization to GDP. The results indicate weak but positive persistence in stock market performance, with the lagged dependent variable remaining insignificant. Although governance indicators are positive but insignificant in the one-step GMM estimates, the two-step Difference GMM results show that control of corruption, regulatory quality, and rule of law significantly enhance stock market performance. Diagnostic tests confirm robustness, underscoring the importance of transparent governance and strong legal frameworks in fostering stock market development.

title: Defense Platform Vulnerability Assessment: Quantifying Rare Earth Supply Chain Risks Across Major Weapons Systems

detail.title: Defense Platform Vulnerability Assessment: Quantifying Rare Earth Supply Chain Risks Across Major Weapons Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author has no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Secondary data use only. No human subjects. Ethics approval granted.
declarations.funderStatement: ICL Institute, New Jersey, USA

detail.abstract: The United States defense industrial base faces an unprecedented strategic vulnerability arising from its critical dependence on rare earth elements (REEs) for advanced weapons systems, combined with China's near-monopolistic control of global REE supply chains. Despite controlling only 38% of global REE reserves, China dominates 68.75% of REE mining, 90% of processing capacity, and 99% of heavy rare earth element (HREE) processing—materials essential for the permanent magnets, guidance systems, and electronic warfare capabilities that define modern military superiority. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) of 4,954 for global REE processing indicates a highly concentrated, monopolistic market structure far exceeding the 2,500 threshold for concern. This quantitative study addressed a critical gap in defense planning by developing and applying a composite vulnerability assessment framework to evaluate REE supply chain risks across 15 major U.S. weapons systems spanning five platform categories: Air (F-35 Lightning II, F-22 Raptor, B-21 Raider, KC-46 Pegasus), Naval (Virginia-class submarine, Columbia-class submarine, DDG-51 destroyer, CVN-78 carrier), Ground (M1 Abrams, JLTV), Munitions (Tomahawk, JDAM, AIM-120 AMRAAM, Patriot), and UAV (Predator/Reaper). The vulnerability index formula V = w₁(REE_content) × w₂(element_criticality) × w₃(1-substitutability) × w₄(strategic_importance) × w₅(1-stockpile_coverage) was applied across three disruption scenarios: Graduated Export Restrictions, Complete HREE Embargo, and Conflict-Induced Supply Cessation. Results revealed naval platforms exhibited the highest category vulnerability (M = 0.7814), with the CVN-78 Ford-class carrier ranking most vulnerable (V = 0.915), followed by Columbia-class (V = 0.793) and Virginia-class submarines (V = 0.743). Ground platforms demonstrated the lowest vulnerability (M = 0.370). Element criticality emerged as the strongest vulnerability driver (r = 0.91), while stockpile coverage provided the strongest protective effect (r = -0.93). Scenario analysis demonstrated that mean platform vulnerability increased from baseline (M = 0.608) by 6.3% under graduated restrictions, 12.2% under HREE embargo, and 22.5% under conflict-induced cessation. These findings provide defense planners with an empirically-grounded framework for prioritizing supply chain mitigation investments, informing strategic stockpile decisions, and guiding industrial base policy to enhance national security resilience.

title: Financial Subordination
affiliations: Stanford Law School

detail.title: Financial Subordination

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Economic regulation has taken on an increasingly partisan valence. Favored companies have their mergers approved, while disfavored ones have their mergers denied. Agencies dedicated to preserving fair competition and protecting consumers in the marketplace have refashioned their authorities into tools to influence cultural issues. Broadcast licenses are available only to companies that toe a certain party line. These are just a few examples of how a certain form of politics has captured the regulatory state. This turn has had particular implications for the financial sector. For a time, the government’s role in ensuring the fair distribution of financial resources was largely viewed in narrow, technocratic, and ostensibly value-neutral terms. The government was responsible for creating money and credit but allocation decisions were delegated to private banks. Conventional wisdom held that normative questions about the aims of financial allocation lay outside regulators’ expertise and remit. The government simply did not “pick winners and losers.” Following the Global Financial Crisis, however, political polarization, shifting societal consensus on issues from climate change to gun control, and changes to administrative law doctrines have injected social consciousness—and partisanship—into financial regulation in new ways. First, banks and policymakers began incorporating issues ranging from climate change to gun safety and racial equity into financial business and policy decisions. A backlash ensued. Certain industries claimed to be the victims of “discrimination” and politicized “de-banking.” State and federal officials used their authorities to keep so-called “woke” values and politics out of finance. We are now living in a normative financial state, wherein partisan and ideological identity is increasingly relevant to financial administration.

This Article begins by offering a synthesis and critical analysis of the trend toward financial subordination. Specifically, it documents how the emergence of popular de-banking folklore distorts a series of reasonable policy choices and responses to societal consensus into something seemingly untoward. This Article argues that conventional narratives that portray “woke” bankers and government agencies engaged in widespread de-banking misrepresent who is being political, how they are doing it, and the deeper implications of these recent moves. It demonstrates that the backlash against “woke” banking is not about protecting vulnerable groups from discrimination or seeking fair and equal access to the banking system. Instead, it is a partisan ideological project consisting of two essential components. It uses debanking folklore to implement measures providing financial access to certain partisan-affiliated groups and causes, while marginalizing non-aligned out-groups. At the same time, the narratives advanced by this project provide pretext for regulatory and deregulatory actions that undermine longstanding banking principles meant to address financial exclusion, emerging financial risks, and illicit financial activity. Looming in the background of these developments are the moves by courts and the Executive Branch to whittle away structural protections that insulate agency policymaking from short-term partisan influence. This Article then considers where financial administration should go from here. It argues that banking regulation and supervision should reflect the longstanding public purposes of ensuring broad access and inclusion and limiting the influence of concentrated financial power.

title: A Computational Framework for Financial Structures
affiliations: CNR - Intitute for Complex Systems

detail.title: A Computational Framework for Financial Structures
detail.abstract: Financial structures transform uncertain cash inflows generated by underlying assets into ordered payments across multiple claims through systems of contractual allocation rules. While sophisticated computational models of such structures are widely used in practice, their allocation logic is typically embedded in proprietary implementations and dealspecific documentation, making systematic analysis, comparison, and verification across transactions difficult. This paper develops a computational framework that formalizes financial structures as structured allocation systems mapping stochastic inflows into hierarchically ordered payments through explicit and state-dependent allocation operators. The framework separates the stochastic generation of inflows from the deterministic and conditional rules governing their distribution across positions, allowing allocation logic, trigger mechanisms, and structural parameters to be represented within a unified computational architecture. This explicit formulation provides a general and transparent representation of how contractual design shapes the distribution of risk and return across claims. Existing modelling approaches typically embed allocation rules within deal-specific implementations, simulation platforms, or pricing environments, where they operate as procedural components rather than as explicit objects of analysis. As a consequence, the structural properties of financial allocation mechanisms — such as priority relations, trigger-driven regime changes, and the mapping from stochastic inflows to distributions of payments — are difficult to characterise or compare independently of particular transactions or software implementations. The representation developed here makes these mechanisms explicit as computable allocation operators. This shift in representation makes it possible to analyse financial structures as parametric and comparable objects, to study how alternative contractual configurations transform identical stochastic inflows into different distributions of payments, and to treat structural design itself as a welldefined computational problem within a unified stochastic environment. In this sense, the framework enables forms of structural analysis and comparison that are difficult to achieve when allocation logic remains embedded in transaction-specific or proprietary modelling architectures. By expressing financial structures as computable allocation systems, the approach supports the derivation of scenario-dependent payment streams, valuation measures, and loss distributions for each position, and enables consistent comparison of alternative structural configurations within a common stochastic environment. More broadly, the formal representation of allocation rules and trigger-driven state transitions provides a foundation for analyzing financial structures as executable and verifiable objects whose behavior can be simulated and inspected across scenarios. The framework thus establishes a unified conceptual and computational language for the analysis, design, and transparent representation of financial structures across asset classes and institutional settings.

title: Rights Assigned, Rewards Denied: Copyright Transfers, Royalty Structures, And The Systemic Exploitation Of Upcoming Nigerian Artists
affiliations: University of Calabar

detail.title: Rights Assigned, Rewards Denied: Copyright Transfers, Royalty Structures, And The Systemic Exploitation Of Upcoming Nigerian Artists
detail.abstract: The Nigerian music industry has experienced unprecedented global growth, driven largely by digital distribution and streaming platforms. Despite this success, upcoming artists remain disproportionately disadvantaged within contractual arrangements with record labels. Central to this imbalance are copyright transfer clauses and opaque royalty structures that effectively strip artists of long-term economic benefits while consolidating control in the hands of labels. This article argues that the exploitation of upcoming Nigerian artists is not merely a function of unequal bargaining power but is structurally embedded within prevailing copyright assignment practices and royalty regimes. Through a doctrinal analysis of the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022, contract law principles, and industry practices, complemented by comparative insights, the paper demonstrates how legal mechanisms intended to facilitate creativity have instead enabled systematic exploitation. It concludes by proposing targeted legislative, contractual, and regulatory reforms aimed at recalibrating the balance between commercial interests and artist protection in Nigeria's music industry.

title: A Network Approach to Interoperability
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - University of International Business and Economics (UIBE), School of International Trade and Economics, Students, University of Southern California - Department of Economics, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Division of Economics and Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: A Network Approach to Interoperability
detail.abstract: We study how interoperability, modeled as a weighted network of connections among competing platforms with user externalities, affects equilibrium prices and welfare. By characterizing equilibrium prices as functions of the eigenvalues of the interoperability network, we derive optimal network configurations and show that industry-wide full interoperability maximizes total welfare and is also platformoptimal. When user externalities are weak, the price effects of interoperability are bounded relative to the direct user-benefit effect, implying that full interoperability is Pareto-optimal. In contrast, coalitional interoperability does not maximize total welfare but can be consumer-optimal when user externalities are strong, as interoperability within coalitions endogenously generates demand complementarities among their members while intensifying competition across coalitions. For the case of four platforms, we fully characterize the set of feasible combinations of profit and consumer surplus and identify the associated Pareto frontier. Overall, the welfare effects of interoperability depend critically on both the strength of user externalities and the structure of interoperability within the industry.

title: Understanding Eu Regional Differences In Agricultural And Manufacturing Gross Value Added Using Drought And Socio-Economic Indicators Via Explainable Machine Learning

detail.title: Understanding Eu Regional Differences In Agricultural And Manufacturing Gross Value Added Using Drought And Socio-Economic Indicators Via Explainable Machine Learning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has declared that he has no competing interests.

detail.abstract: The European Union exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity in economic structure and performance, reflecting divergent historical development trajectories, sectoral composition, socioeconomic conditions, and climatic variability. Among climatic stressors, drought poses a significant challenge to regional economic resilience, particularly in agriculture and manufacturing, which are sensitive to water availability, temperature extremes, and infrastructure constraints. In this study, we quantify the contributions of drought-related and socioeconomic factors to regional gross value added (GVA) across NUTS3 regions in the European Union. We integrate a comprehensive set of climatic indicators from the Copernicus European Drought Observatory with socioeconomic data from Eurostat, and apply an eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model coupled with Shapley value-based interpretability methods to attribute sector-specific economic outcomes to individual features. Our analysis reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in the contributions of socioeconomic and climatic factors to GVA. Variability in both agricultural and manufacturing GVA is predominantly explained by socioeconomic factors. Agricultural GVA is largely influenced by the employment share in agriculture and regional area, reflecting the availability of labour and land resources, while manufacturing GVA is strongly associated with overall regional economic performance, as proxied by gross domestic product. Among climatic drivers, winter temperature-a critical factor for plant survival-explains the largest share of variability in agricultural GVA, with soil moisture and vegetation photosynthetic activity, used here as proxies for productivity, also contributing. For manufacturing, the median monthly maximum temperature emerges as the most influential climatic variable, with soil moisture and photosynthetic activity contributing as secondary predictors. However, in the manufacturing sector, these climatic associations likely reflect spatial covariation with regional characteristics rather than direct causal impacts of climate on production processes.

title: Nonlinear Victoria-Nash Equilibrium: Curvature and Stability in Asymmetric Systems
affiliations: Royal Statistical Society

detail.title: Nonlinear Victoria-Nash Equilibrium: Curvature and Stability in Asymmetric Systems
detail.abstract: We introduce the Victoria-Nash manifold Γ V N AE (θ) as a smooth submanifold arising from an asymmetric expectation field F (s; θ). With a Riemannian metric g(θ) and curvature K(s; θ) encoding asymmetry via a smooth structural field ϕ(s; θ), Γ V N AE generalizes Nash and von Neumann equilibria. We prove existence, smoothness, and invariance using Lefschetz, Tikhonov, and Lyapunov-Morse theory. Classical equilibria are degenerate limits at K → 0.

title: The Future of Gender Equality in the EU
affiliations: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), ETUI, European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) and European Trade Union Institute (ETUI)

detail.title: The Future of Gender Equality in the EU

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Gender equality is a core value of the European Union (EU), a fundamental right enshrined in the EU Treaties and a key principle of the European Pillar of Social Rights (EPSR). A central policy instrument in this area is the Gender Equality Strategy (GES). Formulated as a five-year plan, it frames the European Commission’s work on gender equality and sets out policy objectives and key actions. 

This Report aims to demonstrate the nature of the progress the EU has made towards gender equality in recent years, identify areas where further improvement is required and propose the most effective strategies for achieving genuine and lasting progress. Its analysis focuses on two areas: policy and regulatory changes; and labour market trends in the key aspects of gender inequality. The objective is to provide a comprehensive knowledge base on genderrelated developments by synthesising key policy changes and providing rich empirical evidence to highlight the significant risks and concerns.

The Report’s overview of labour market trends provides nuance to the headline indicators cited in EU policy documents, revealing what underlies some of the observed changes and enabling a better understanding of the nature of the gender gaps, and identifies more effective ways of capturing inequalities between men and women. The evidence is then used to evaluate and engage critically with future EU-level policy priorities for achieving gender equality.

title: The Clause that can Kill a Deal: Understanding Change of Control in M&A
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Clause that can Kill a Deal: Understanding Change of Control in M&A
detail.abstract: Change of control clauses regulate how contractual rights and obligations respond to shifts in corporate ownership and control, making them a critical consideration in mergers and acquisitions. This short note analyses the meaning, function, and transactional impact of such clauses, highlighting their role in triggering consent requirements, termination rights, and deal execution risks. Through a concise and practical discussion, this note seeks to enhance understanding of why change of control clauses often operate as decisive deal-shaping mechanisms in M&A transactions.

title: Understanding Classical Decomposability of Inequality Measures: A Graphical Analysis

detail.title: Understanding Classical Decomposability of Inequality Measures: A Graphical Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper's objective is pedagogical and interpretive. Namely,  it gives a simple  geometric analysis of classical (by which I mean population-share-weighted or income-share-weighted) inequality decomposability in the simplest nontrivial setting of  three individuals.  Income distributions in this case can  be represented as points on the two-dimensional income-share simplex. In this representation, classical  decomposability translates into concrete geometric restrictions of within- and between-group components. The geometric framework makes it possible to localize and compare violations of decomposability across inequality measures. The analysis is applied to the Mean Log Deviation, the Gini coefficient, the coefficient of variation, and the Theil index.

title: EU Mobility and Persons with Disabilities: Removing Barriers to Free Movement, Work and Social Protection
affiliations: University of Salamanca and Catholic University of Ávila

detail.title: EU Mobility and Persons with Disabilities: Removing Barriers to Free Movement, Work and Social Protection

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Despite steps taken in recent years to protect the rights of workers and jobseekers with disabilities, they still face numerous barriers to exercising their right to cross-border mobility between European Union (EU) Member States. To this end, data on people with disabilities in Europe was analysed, the views of organisations representing their rights were collected, and EU policies were reviewed to assess the main factors hindering their mobility and the exportability of social benefits between Member States. Moreover, this research also aims to lay the groundwork for the creation of a comprehensive database, which does not yet exist at European level, including information on the number of people with disabilities, especially jobseekers and workers, who move annually between EU countries, or the estimated number of workers with disabilities who have been able legally and effectively to export their social benefits. The study concludes with recommendations on the enforcement of the rights of people with disabilities in all Member States, to ensure that they can travel, study and work throughout the EU.

title: Behavioral Responses to Risk: Evidence from Classified Ads

detail.title: Behavioral Responses to Risk: Evidence from Classified Ads
detail.abstract: Measuring behavioral responses to risk is challenging when behaviors are private and unobserved. Using 170,000 classified ads from a national LGBT publication (1975-1992), I examine responses to emerging HIV/AIDS risk. Exploiting variation in timing of first AIDS cases across cities, I find heterogeneous responses: relationship-seeking ads declined sharply, while explicitly sexual ads were less responsive. Simultaneously, safe-sex requests increased, and cities with greater adoption experienced larger declines in male syphilis rates. These findings reveal that perceived risk produces divergent behavioral responses across different segments of the market, with some populations exiting entirely while others adapt their practices in place.

title: Here Comes the Sun: The Formal Transposition and Political Impact of the European Directive on Adequate Minimum Wages in the EU
affiliations: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI)

detail.title: Here Comes the Sun: The Formal Transposition and Political Impact of the European Directive on Adequate Minimum Wages in the EU

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
As the first ever piece of EU legislation aimed explicitly at ensuring adequate minimum wages and promoting strong collective bargaining, the European Directive on Adequate Minimum Wages in the EU is a milestone in strengthening the social dimension of the European Union. Its ultimate policy objective is to reduce wage inequality and in-work poverty in order to advance upward social convergence and social cohesion across the EU. Because of the EU's limited competences on the issue of wages and collective bargaining, however, while the Directive is strong on procedural regulations it is weaker on substantive requirements, which are formulated mainly in terms of recommendations. This is why the real impact of the Directive in the sense of achieving its political objectives relies strongly on an ambitious transposition into national law that transforms the ‘soft law' of the Directive into hard law at national level.

One dimension of the analysis therefore concerns how the Member States have formally transposed the Directive into national law. However, the comprehensive formal transposition of the Directive is only one factor that will determine its success in realising its political objectives. The other important factor is the Directive's broader political implications as manifested in its influence on the political agenda and the political and public discourse about minimum wages and collective bargaining in the Member States. This report deals with both dimensions of the impact of the European Minimum Wage Directive.

title: René Favaloro: construction, use, and discard of the myth

detail.title: René Favaloro: construction, use, and discard of the myth
detail.abstract: This work analyzes the René Favaloro case as a structural problem of narrative production and not as a biographical or moral controversy. The central hypothesis holds that an infantile epic systematically substitutes for the technically verifiable reconstruction of the surgical training prior to his entry into the Cleveland Clinic. The analysis shifts the focus from individual exceptionalism toward the material, organizational, and documentary conditions necessary to produce high-complexity surgical competence in a given historical context. When those conditions leave no marks, the account ceases to be professional history and begins to operate as a functional fable.

title: Are We Prepared for America's Aging Reality? An Independent Health Policy Analysis

detail.title: Are We Prepared for America's Aging Reality? An Independent Health Policy Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently without financial support from any organization.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: The United States is approaching a demographic inflection point as more than 73 million Baby Boomers age into a healthcare system largely structured around hospital-based, episodic care. This independent policy analysis examines the structural mismatch between current aging care infrastructure and projected demand through 2030, with attention to workforce constraints, rising institutional care costs, and limitations in system scalability. Using secondary data and comparative policy analysis conducted between 2024 and early 2026, the study identifies a critical gap: the absence of continuous, preventive oversight for older adults who are clinically stable but at elevated risk of deterioration. This gap creates a structural vulnerability where early warning signs go undetected, leading to preventable crises that burden emergency departments and drive hospital admissions, averaging $13,000-$17,000 per episode. The analysis evaluates proactive Remote Care Management (RCM) approaches as a potential strategy to support earlier risk identification and home-based intervention. Evidence from pilot programs and Medicare demonstration projects suggests that continuous monitoring costs approximately $50-$75 per patient per month, substantially lower than institutional alternatives, while enabling earlier clinical intervention. Strengthening continuous monitoring capacity could reduce avoidable hospital utilization while extending the effective capacity of existing care teams. The brief concludes with three policy recommendations: (1) expanding Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement for preventive monitoring, (2) prioritizing investment in scalable home-based care infrastructure, and (3) establishing interoperability standards to support integration of home-generated health data into routine clinical care. Together, these actions provide a policy pathway to improve system sustainability and support aging in place as demographic pressures accelerate.

title: Institutional Architecture of Privilege: The Epstein-Mount Sinai Case

detail.title: Institutional Architecture of Privilege: The Epstein-Mount Sinai Case
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes a set of documents released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act in order to assess whether the interactions between Jeffrey Epstein and the Mount Sinai Health System constitute isolated episodes of preferential treatment or the consistent operation of an institutional architecture of privilege. Drawing on clinical, administrative, and procedural evidence, the analysis shows that the system does not rely on contingent personal favors but on formal and semi-formal circuits capable of absorbing sensitive demands, operating effectively outside ordinary workflows, and simultaneously preserving opacity against attempts at documentary reconstruction. The analysis does not assert direct illegality; it establishes institutional density, capacity for exception, and preventive shielding.

title: Learning-Based Portfolio Policies as Approximations to Risk-Sensitive Stochastic Control

detail.title: Learning-Based Portfolio Policies as Approximations to Risk-Sensitive Stochastic Control

keywords: financial decision systems. JEL Classification. C61 (Optimization Techniques)

detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for risk-sensitive stochastic control tailored to modern banking applications. Classical control theory focuses on expectation-based objectives, whereas financial institutions operate under coherent and regulatory risk measures such as Expected Shortfall. We formulate a general control framework in which nonlinear risk mappings replace expectations, leading to dynamic programming equations driven by coherent risk functionals. We establish the dual interpretation of risk-sensitive control as robust optimization over distorted probability measures and analyze both discrete-time and continuous-time settings. The framework is extended to learning-based policy approximation, where Bellman residual bounds provide explicit links between statistical errors and economic performance degradation. A central contribution of the paper is the translation of risk-sensitive control theory into practical banking contexts. We analyze implications across equities, rates, foreign exchange, and credit portfolios, showing how coherent risk objectives reshape optimal policies under liquidity, macro-regime, and jump-risk dynamics. We further reinterpret regulatory constructs such as FRTB Expected Shortfall and P&L attribution tests as implicit stability constraints on control policies. The results provide a mathematically grounded bridge between stochastic control, reinforcement learning, and banking regulation, offering a foundation for robust decision-making under distributional uncertainty.

title: Monetary Policy Surprises and the Cross Sectional Stock Return Predictability in Volume Sorted Portfolios
affiliations: University Texas at San Antonio

detail.title: Monetary Policy Surprises and the Cross Sectional Stock Return Predictability in Volume Sorted Portfolios
detail.abstract: The predictive power of monetary policy for the aggregate stock market has been well documented. This paper provides the first empirical evidence on whether monetary policy also predicts/explains any existing return anomalies (cross sectional return predictability) that figure prominently in the asset price literature. The results show that the Fed's forward guidance helps predict the volume premium, a notion that stocks that recently receive a substantial positive volume shock earn higher average returns. In contrast, current monetary policy action does not predict the return anomaly. Furthermore, the predictive power of monetary policy adopted after the unscheduled FOMC meetings is twice as strong as that following the scheduled meetings. Nevertheless, the predictive relation is statistically insignificant in the zero lower bound (ZLB) period.

title: What Do Medicaid Fraud Classifiers Actually Detect?

detail.title: What Do Medicaid Fraud Classifiers Actually Detect?
detail.abstract: Publicly available Medicaid claims data cannot distinguish providers excluded for fraud from providers excluded for non-fraud reasons such as license revocation. Using the HHS Medicaid Provider Spending dataset (227 million records, 488,030 providers, 2018-2024), the OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities, and CMS provider registry data, we construct a supervised classification framework with temporal outof-sample validation to test whether billing patterns in public data can screen for fraud. The best classifier (random forest) achieves AUC-ROC 0.830 on a temporal holdout. This performance reflects provider volume and practice duration; fraud-specific billing patterns play no role. All top-ranked features predict fraud through lower values. Behavioral billing features contribute only 16 percent of model importance and achieve near-random discrimination (AUC 0.589) when used alone. A placebo test using non-fraud exclusions produces a statistically indistinguishable AUC of 0.852 (DeLong p = 0.91). The classifier detects provider size alone. Temporal trajectory features (billing slopes, acceleration, structural breaks) reduce performance from AUC 0.830 to 0.820, and analysis of pre-exclusion billing reveals that spending declines begin 15-18 months before exclusion, tracking the investigation and enforcement process. These findings establish that the binding constraint on public-data fraud screening is data granularity: investment in data infrastructure may yield higher returns than investment in algorithms applied to suppressed data.

title: The Importance of Audit Partner-Client Matches in Explaining Audit Quality and Fees
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business and Pennsylvania State University - Department of Accounting

detail.title: The Importance of Audit Partner-Client Matches in Explaining Audit Quality and Fees
detail.abstract: Audit partners are not assigned to their clients randomly. We investigate the economic importance of these partner-client matches in explaining audit quality and audit fees. Using a three way mixed-effect model to quantify the effect of these matches, we find that they explain a sizeable amount of the variation in audit quality and fees. Match effects explain substantially more variation in audit quality than individual partner effects do when considering typical measures, such as restatements and discretionary accruals. Match effects on audit quality are also complements rather than substitutes to client and partner effects. Further analyses suggest that early audit partner rotations are more likely when the match on audit quality is worse, consistent with both client and auditor incentives for higher audit quality. We also find some evidence that capital markets value matches that result in greater quality audits. Overall, our results underscore the importance of audit partner-client match effects in explaining audit quality and audit fees.

title: Heterogeneous Agents In Developed and Developing Countries

detail.title: Heterogeneous Agents In Developed and Developing Countries
detail.abstract: I study whether an economy’s response to aggregate shocks depends on its level of development. Empirically, I estimate responses to high-frequency monetary shocks at the macro and micro level and compute hand-tomouth shares for high, middle and low income countries. An inverted U-shaped relationship between these two is found. Theoretically, I show that matching this relationship requires a heterogeneous agent model with one key feature: countercyclical inequality and income risk. This generates amplifying income effects by shifting towards constrained households the additional aggregate demand generated by unconstrained households’ substitution effects. Amplification peaks with heterogeneity, when there is an equal share of households on and off their Euler equations. These results have implications for aggregate demand stabilization policies and the welfare costs of business cycles.

title: Growth without Profits: How will ‘Involution’ in China End?
affiliations: Bruegel and Bruegel

detail.title: Growth without Profits: How will ‘Involution’ in China End?
detail.abstract: This paper analyses China's economic 'involution' , a phenomenon characterised by intense competition in overcrowded markets such as electric vehicles (EVs), price wars, declining profit margins and ongoing resource misallocation via 'zombie firms'. Using data from Chinese listed companies, we decompose firm profits and find that, while firm-level total factor productivity (TFP) has risen since 2020, markups are falling. More granularly, firms across the productivity spectrum are compressing their profit margins to compete for market share. The fact that even companies without productivity gains are lowering prices has contributed to a growing share of lossmaking zombie firms, which survive on the back of bank support or government subsidies, hindering consolidation. China's policy efforts emphasise anti-involution measures including regulation of predatory pricing and promotion of orderly exits, but they have not yet solved the fundamental problem, as unproductive firms continue to operate. For Europe, this has heightened the concern that China's involution-driven growth model is fuelling export expansion through persistent low-price competition, increasing the likelihood that the EU will strengthen its trade-defence measures, alongside efforts to raise its own productivity.

title: Firm Level Heterogeneity and the Impact of Monetary Policy on Labour Demand
affiliations: , European Central Bank (ECB) and Banque de France

detail.title: Firm Level Heterogeneity and the Impact of Monetary Policy on Labour Demand

publicationDetails.journalName: National Bank of Belgium Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Monetary policy asymmetrically affects the response of firms’ employment to an output shock and plays a role in cushioning employment adjustment over the business cycle. Combining annual firmlevel data until 2020 with quarterly firm-level data until 2023 and highfrequency monetary policy surprises, we show that for a given change in output, monetary policy influences the extent to which firms hold on to labour, or “labour hoard”. Furthermore, this effect is asymmetric: a restrictive monetary policy reduces labour hoarding behaviour by 2 to 3 times more than an accommodative policy increases it. Finally, we look at the role of financing conditions and firm demographics.

title: Reverse-Engineering Kuwait's Currency Basket: A Frankel–Wei Analysis with Out-of-Sample Validation

detail.title: Reverse-Engineering Kuwait's Currency Basket: A Frankel–Wei Analysis with Out-of-Sample Validation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflicts of interest to disclose. The author may hold positions in currencies discussed in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Central Bank of Kuwait pegs the dinar to an undisclosed currency basket. We reverse-engineer its composition using 937 weekly observations (March 2008–February 2026) and the Frankel and Wei (1994) framework, augmented by a two-stage design: LASSO penalized regression first screens 20 non-KWD candidate currencies and Brent crude to select basket members with minimal prior assumptions, then constrained OLS estimates the weights. The basket is 84.5% USD, 10.5% EUR, 3.0% JPY, and 2.0% GBP, all statistically significant, including GBP, whose small but robust weight survives across all sub-periods, bandwidths, and numeraire choices. Weights frozen from a 70% training sample and applied blind to the remaining 30% deliver an out-of-sample R² of 0.9885, confirming that the basket has remained stable through the global financial crisis, the 2014–2015 oil price collapse, COVID-19, and 525 basis points of Fed tightening. The near-84% dollar weight reveals that the dinar is de facto a soft dollar peg despite its formal basket label, leaving Kuwait's exchange rate overwhelmingly dollar-determined.

title: China's Critical Technology Surge: A Contested Ascent
affiliations: Bruegel

detail.title: China's Critical Technology Surge: A Contested Ascent
detail.abstract: This report examines China's remarkable ascent in frontier innovation across artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and quantum computing, demonstrating how the world's second-largest economy is rapidly closing the technological gap with the United States. While the US maintains overall leadership, China has achieved significant progress and even parity in key subfields of these three critical technologies. However, this ascent is contested and fraught with challenges. China's state-driven industrial policy, while effective in mobilizing resources, has also led to inefficiencies, waste, and a reliance on foreign technology in critical upstream segments, particularly in semiconductors. US-led export controls have created significant bottlenecks, forcing Chinese firms to innovate around constraints. The US clearly needs to step up efforts while using its alliances more forcefully in terms of technological cooperation. As for Europe, to avoid further marginalization, Europe and other global actors must learn from both the successes and failures of China's model, focusing on strategic coordination, market integration, and multilateral collaboration to foster resilient and competitive innovation ecosystems.

title: The Microstructure of NFT Markets: Evidence from 410 Million Orderbook Events
affiliations: University of Ulm - Department of Mathematics and Economics

detail.title: The Microstructure of NFT Markets: Evidence from 410 Million Orderbook Events
detail.abstract: Non-Fungible Token (NFT) trading volumes are in the tens of billions. We provide the first comprehensive analysis of NFT market microstructure using orderbook data, analyzing over 410 million bid, ask, sale, and transfer events across six major Ethereum-based NFT collections. We introduce a framework for two-tier orderbooks in which collection-level bids, rather than token-specific bids, supply the dominant source of buy-side liquidity. Median quoted spreads range from 48% to approximately 200%, yet floor-benchmark spreads - measuring how far sale prices deviate from the daily median collection-level bid - are substantially lower (2-5% for liquid collections), revealing that wide quoted spreads partly reflect structural properties of collection-level bidding rather than round-trip transaction costs. A small number of algorithmic market makers (5 to 38 per collection) supply the bulk of liquidity but face adverse selection in collection-level offers: Tokens sold into floor bids are less rare, though the dominant risk is market-wide price declines.

title: Can Polymarket Become a More Accurate "Survey"? A Replacement for Traditional Surveys That Are Easy to Game?
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Can Polymarket Become a More Accurate "Survey"? A Replacement for Traditional Surveys That Are Easy to Game?
detail.abstract: Traditional surveys often face incentive problems: respondents may answer carelessly, answer just to finish quickly (especially in paid surveys), or answer according to social desirability without any direct consequence. Prediction markets such as Polymarket offer an alternative mechanism: participants stake their own money, so incorrect predictions have real costs. Academic literature suggests that prediction markets are often quite accurate and, in many contexts, can outperform polling-especially at longer time horizons. This paper (i) explains how Polymarket works (binary contracts, USDC collateral on Polygon, a CLOB order book mechanism, and oracle-based resolution), (ii) summarizes empirical evidence from the broader prediction-market literature, and (iii) incorporates quantitative findings from Polymarket data studies. An important note: when a market's resolution criteria are ambiguous, the price is often better interpreted as the probability that the market will be resolved as Yes under the stated rules, rather than the probability that the underlying real-world event "truly" happened [20, 19, 16]. For example, Chen et al. (2024) analyze more than 15,000 addresses across 4,500 events and 8,500 markets [21], while Saguillo et al. (2025) report an estimated realized arbitrage profit of about $40 million [22]. All factual numbers/claims in this paper are stated as results according to the cited sources, not as independent claims by the author. However, prediction markets are not "pure truth": participant bias, liquidity, contract design and resolution definitions, and manipulation risks (price impact, wash trading, and oraclemechanism attacks) can limit how prices should be interpreted as probabilities.

reference: Richard D. Pomp & Monika Gradzki, Sales Taxes in the United States - Historical Development and Policy Analysis, 5 Warsaw L. Rev. 86 (2006).
title: Sales Taxes in the United States — Historical Development and Policy Analysis
affiliations: University of Connecticut - School of Law and University of Szczecin

detail.title: Sales Taxes in the United States — Historical Development and Policy Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Richard D. Pomp & Monika Gradzki, Sales Taxes in the United States - Historical Development and Policy Analysis, 5 Warsaw L. Rev. 86 (2006).

detail.abstract:
Sales taxes have become one of the most significant sources of revenue for state governments in the United States, accounting for nearly half of aggregate state tax revenues when general and selective sales taxes are considered together. In “Sales Taxes in the United States — Historical Development and Policy Analysis,” authors Richard D. Pomp and Monika Gradzki offer a comprehensive examination of the historical development, structural design, and policy challenges of state sales taxes that can inform the value added taxes, which are simply a sales tax collected in stages. The Article begins with its origins during the Great Depression, when widespread fiscal crises and demands for property tax relief prompted the adoption of general retail sales taxes as “temporary” measures, which soon became entrenched as permanent revenue instruments. By the late 1960s, forty-five states had enacted such taxes—none in recent times.

The article analyzes the trajectory of sales tax rates, which have risen substantially since their inception, offsetting the relative stagnation of the tax base. It highlights serious challenges to sales tax driven by three forces: (1) the systematic exemption of personal services, despite their growing share of household consumption; (2) the inconsistent and often regressive taxation of business inputs and investment-related activities, resulting in higher effective tax burdens on consumers through cascading (often inappropriately called pyramiding); and (3) prior to Wayfair, weak compliance with the use tax, particularly in the context of interstate commerce, remote vendors, and transactions by mail, telephone, or the Internet. Case studies illustrate both the deliberate policy choices and the unintended consequences that shape contemporary administration of sales taxes.

Pomp and Gradzki also explore policy debates over regressivity, neutrality, and the use of temporary sales tax holidays, examining these alongside the broader question of whether the sales tax structure adequately reflects modern patterns of consumption. The concluding sections evaluate the Streamlined Sales Tax Project (SSTP), a multistate initiative launched in 2000 to simplify and modernize sales and use tax collection and administration. It aims to do so by creating uniform definitions, sourcing rules, and rate structures across jurisdictions. The SSTP represents an important effort to modernize sales and use tax administration in light of e-commerce and constitutional constraints, but the high-population states have not joined. 

Through historical context and policy analysis, the study highlights both the enduring significance of the sales tax and the persistent obstacles to its equitable and efficient administration.

title: Mergers and R&D Investment: A Unified Approach
affiliations: and VU University Amsterdam - Department of Economics

detail.title: Mergers and R&D Investment: A Unified Approach
detail.abstract: We investigate the impact of mergers on R&D incentives within a framework of R&D competition where effort can influence both the probability of innovation and the payoff conditional on success. Our framework nests the results of two classes of existing models and reveals assumptions that are restrictive. In models where R&D effort increases the probability of innovation but does not directly affect the payoff upon success, we show that the assumption of zero payoff upon innovation failure is restrictive. In models where R&D effort influences the payoff conditional on success, but not the probability of success itself, the assumption of deterministic innovation success (i.e., a success probability of one) is similarly restrictive. Across both modeling approaches, we offer a novel insight: the shape of investment costs, and by implication the pre-merger level of innovation, can be pivotal in determining whether a merger strengthens or weakens firms' incentives to invest in R&D. In an extensions section, we further examine the role of R&D input and output synergies, firm asymmetries, as well as the implications for consumer surplus.

title: How Much Change Is Needed? Mapping Global EAT-Lancet Diet Transitions
affiliations: Waseda University

detail.title: How Much Change Is Needed? Mapping Global EAT-Lancet Diet Transitions
detail.abstract: Global dietary change is increasingly promoted as a way to reduce pressure on planetary boundaries, yet most global assessments rely on uniform adoption scenarios that overlook important feasibility constraints. This study develops a global optimization framework to identify the minimum dietary shift toward the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet needed to meet environmental targets while remaining nutritionally adequate and affordable across countries. Using FAO food balance data and consumption-based environmental footprints from a multiregional inputoutput framework, we show that near-maximal environmental gains can be achieved without universal adoption. The optimized pathway reduces food-related greenhouse gas emissions by 25.9%, blue water use by 22.6%, and agricultural land demand by 32.1%, while requiring dietary adjustment by only 65.8% of the global population in population-weighted terms. Optimal adoption rates vary widely across countries and are driven primarily by binding nutritional and affordability constraints rather than baseline environmental intensity. These findings highlight the importance of differentiated, context-specific dietary policies supported by broader affordability and food-system interventions.

title: When Order-by-Order Auctions Meet AMMs: Information Leakage, Sniping, and Flow Selection
affiliations: The University of Tokyo

detail.title: When Order-by-Order Auctions Meet AMMs: Information Leakage, Sniping, and Flow Selection
detail.abstract: Order-flow auctions (OFAs) are increasingly being introduced on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to complement Automated market makers (AMMs). In practice, however, OFAs often leak partial order information to dealers before the auction clears. This paper studies how such leakage, through dealers' bid/abstain and sniping decisions, feeds back into equilibrium AMM liquidity depth when liquidity providers enter competitively. We develop a one-period, single-asset model with informed and uninformed traders who choose between routing directly to an AMM and submitting to an OFA. Upon OFA submission, each dealer observes a private signal about order toxicity and chooses whether to bid or abstain, and abstaining dealers may attempt to snipe the AMM. If the OFA fails, the order falls back to the AMM and may face additional slippage or execution failure risk. The model delivers three results: (i) leakage creates an "abstain → snipe" option, implying cutoff participation and lower fill rates for more toxic orders; (ii) endogenous routing induces flow sorting that can raise AMM toxicity and reduce equilibrium depth under free entry; and (iii) direction hiding weakens sniping incentives, improves fill outcomes, and mitigates the fallback externality, expanding the volatility region in which OFA generates price improvement.

title: Closed Obligation Bilateral Loops in Agent-Based Economies: Stability Under Shock

detail.title: Closed Obligation Bilateral Loops in Agent-Based Economies: Stability Under Shock

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or personal data and therefore does not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
We develop a bilateral obligation framework in which agents maintain symmetric commitments: an obligation to deliver and a binding obligation to accept delivery. Coordination in this architecture is governed by enforceable commitments backed by deposits, rather than relying exclusively on price adjustment mechanisms.

The model is benchmarked against standard bilateral exchange under stochastic default conditions using agent-based Monte Carlo simulations. We evaluate cascade dynamics, cumulative throughput loss, and stability boundaries across enforcement regimes. Results show that symmetric enforcement significantly reduces cascade propagation, lowers systemic throughput losses during shocks, and expands the stability region of the network.

Phase-space analysis reveals a monotonic relationship between enforcement intensity and systemic resilience, indicating that commitment symmetry operates as a structural stabilizer in decentralized exchange systems.

By formalizing commitment-mediated coordination as an endogenous enforcement mechanism, the framework contributes to institutional economics and market design, identifying conditions under which obligation-centered architectures enhance robustness in networked markets.

title: Flooding the Market? How Hurricanes Impact Home Listings
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and Federal Reserve Board of Governors

detail.title: Flooding the Market? How Hurricanes Impact Home Listings
detail.abstract: The lack of an emerging consensus regarding how home prices respond to natural disasters presents a puzzle: Why do some analyses find increases while others find decreases? We develop a model illustrating how transaction composition shifts between "safe" and "risky" homes can yield positive price effect estimates and declining quantities even when shocks decrease values of homes more broadly. Using property-level disaster risk, treatment, and real estate listing and sales data, we implement a novel approach focusing on listings started immediately before an event in order to limit the role of selection bias. In this sample, we find non-elevated flooded homes are 10 percent less likely to sell while elevated homes in the wider region are 1.4 percent more likely to sell. Listings for non-elevated flooded homes that do end up selling spend over five weeks more on the market and are nine percent more likely to sell at large discounts. We further find that flooded homes listed after the year landfall are more likely to have elevated foundations and less likely to have upgraded features. We also find support for the hypothesis that disasters cause shrink housing market supply, as local projections point to temporary disruptions in listings and sales that are not made up later. These supply effects are more pronounced in more severely flooded Census tracts. Extreme weather events can cause sample selection bias in sales, a phenomenon known as "transaction bias" that can skew price effect estimates and may explain some of the disagreement in the price effect research.

title: Flat-Rate Medicaid Reimbursement and Geographic Variation in Provider Participation: Evidence from California

detail.title: Flat-Rate Medicaid Reimbursement and Geographic Variation in Provider Participation: Evidence from California

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract:
Objective: To quantify geographic and specialty-level variation in Medi-Cal provider participation rates across California's 58 counties and examine the relationship between local practice costs and provider engagement with the program.

Data Sources: NPPES provider registry (2024); HHS Medicaid Provider Spending dataset (January 2018–December 2024); composite practice cost index from BLS wage data, HUD Fair Market Rents, and healthcare purchased services indices.

Study Design: Descriptive analysis of provider participation rates, pooled over a seven-year period (2018–2024), defined as the share of NPPES-registered providers in each county who actively billed Medi-Cal during the study period. Rates were stratified by county, Hospital Referral Region (HRR), and six specialty categories.

Principal Findings: Among 79,223 NPPES-registered providers across California's 58 counties, 31,798 (40.1%) actively billed Medi-Cal. County-level participation ranged from 0% (Sierra County, N=2 providers) to 48.3% (Marin County). Bay Area counties with the highest practice costs (composite cost index 162–186) paradoxically exhibited higher participation (44–48%) than low-cost rural counties (17–30%), suggesting that provider density and institutional infrastructure may matter more than reimbursement adequacy alone. Behavioral health had the lowest median participation (27.3%) across all specialties, with the vast majority of counties clustered between 25% and 29%. Low overall participation (<34%) clusters along the Central Valley and far-north I-5 corridor, with four HRRs (Bakersfield, Modesto, Stockton, and Redding) covering approximately 3.6 million residents.

Conclusions: Medi-Cal's flat-rate reimbursement, which unlike Medicare's GPCI makes no geographic adjustment, produces predictable gaps in provider participation. The positive association between practice costs and participation suggests urban institutional infrastructure buffers against low reimbursement in ways unavailable to rural communities. Geographic payment adjustment and targeted behavioral health investments warrant consideration as states implement new CMS network adequacy requirements. Data are available at https://www.caphegroup.org/tools/access-explorer.

title: Multivariate Time Series Classification With Online Expert Advice: An Application to Market Regimes
affiliations: and Credit Agricole Assurances

detail.title: Multivariate Time Series Classification With Online Expert Advice: An Application to Market Regimes
detail.abstract:
Market regimes are critical for tactical asset allocation and risk management, yet their subjective nature has prevented a consensus definition. This paper confronts this ambiguity by introducing a systematic framework for ex-ante cross-asset market regime identification, framing the challenge as a binary classification problem with highly imbalanced data. The framework is designed to be cross-asset, allowing for a flexible definition of the underlying risk factor and leveraging machine learning to incorporate diverse economic and financial features. 

A supervised learning pipeline is implemented on the equity risk factor using four distinct classifiers-Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and a multi-layer perceptron, trained on a rich dataset of macroeconomic and market variables. To enhance predictive stability and robustness, online convex optimization algorithms, such as Exponentially Weighted Average (EWA) and Online Gradient Descent (OGD), were employed to implement an expert-advice framework that dynamically updates the weights of each classifier based on its performance. 

The ensemble approach demonstrates a significant improvement over a traditional Hidden Markov Model (HMM) benchmark. The OGD ensemble model increased the F1-score from 51% to 80% and reduced the Brier score from 20% to 14%, showing a superior ability to classify market regimes and predict upcoming stress. Furthermore, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis provided deep interpretability, revealing that macroeconomic indicators-particularly inflation, are primary drivers of equity market regimes. The analysis also highlighted the unique ability of the neural network to identify upcoming stress signals. 

Overall, this paper proves that combining multiple machine learning models within an expert-advice scheme yields a robust, interpretable, and adaptable solution for market regime detection, offering valuable insights for tactical asset allocation, risk management and systematic hedging strategies.

title: The Fiscal Fracture: Property Tax Erosion and the Municipal Consequences of the Boomer Asset Mirage

detail.title: The Fiscal Fracture: Property Tax Erosion and the Municipal Consequences of the Boomer Asset Mirage
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Fiscal Channel, a third mechanism of the Cohort Asset Circularity Trap first described in the companion paper “The Boomer Asset Mirage” (Hanley, 2026). The Fiscal Channel identifies the pathway through which demographically-driven residential property value declines erode the property tax base that funds local government services and public education in communities where Baby Boomer homeownership is concentrated and working-age in-migration is insufficient to absorb the supply of housing released by boomer demographic exit.

Property taxes constitute between 70 and 75 percent of all local government tax revenue in the United States, including school district collections, and fund approximately 35 percent of national K–12 public education spending. According to U.S. Census Bureau data, state and local governments collected a record $797 billion in property tax revenue in 2024, representing 38 percent of all state and local tax collections. This revenue base is structurally vulnerable to a sustained, geographically concentrated decline in residential assessed values of the kind the Boomer Asset Mirage framework projects.

We document a self-reinforcing dynamic we term the Fiscal Circularity Loop: declining boomer-driven property values reduce municipal and school district tax bases; reduced revenues degrade public services and school quality; degraded services reduce community attractiveness to working-age households; reduced in-migration suppresses housing demand; and further demand suppression drives additional value declines. This loop mirrors the broader Cohort Asset Circularity Trap at the local government scale and represents one of the most durable and least-examined structural fiscal risks of the coming two decades.

Regional exposure to the Fiscal Channel is acute in northern New England, where Maine, Vermont, and New Hampshire hold the three highest median ages among all U.S. states. New Hampshire funds 70 percent of local public education through locally-retained property taxes and ranks dead last among all states in state contribution to public education at 28.8 percent, making its school finance system uniquely exposed to residential assessed value declines. Vermont’s K–12 enrollment has fallen 26 percent since 2003–2004, and the state’s rural school districts are already being described by regional media and state officials as experiencing a “death spiral” of enrollment loss, fixed-cost inflation, and property tax increases that accelerate out-migration — a live demonstration of the Fiscal Circularity Loop in early motion.

The paper extends the analysis to rural communities broadly, aging inner-ring suburbs, and coastal vacation markets where boomer-dominated second-home supply will simultaneously contract municipal tax bases and reduce the discretionary buyer demand that sustained those markets. Policy responses examined include regional tax base sharing, circuit breaker reforms, state equalization restructuring, and strategic land use and revitalization investment.

We find that no existing research integrates demographic cohort-exit dynamics, residential housing supply, and local government fiscal outcomes in a unified analytical framework. We call for a multi-disciplinary research program — initiated before the peak of the boomer demographic transition — to map regional fiscal exposure and model fiscal impacts under a range of supply and demand scenarios.

title: How to Save Lives Across the Globe: The Limits of Smoking Harm Education and the Promise of Market Driven Harm Reduction

detail.title: How to Save Lives Across the Globe: The Limits of Smoking Harm Education and the Promise of Market Driven Harm Reduction

detail.abstract: Cigarette smoking remains one of the leading causes of preventable mortality worldwide, causing several million deaths annually, most of them in low-and middle-income countries. Although the health risks of smoking have been widely known for decades, smoking prevalence has declined slowly in many regions and has plateaued in others. This persistence cannot plausibly be explained primarily by lack of awareness. Instead, it reflects institutional and market constraints that limit smokers' ability to substitute combustible cigarettes with substantially lower-risk nicotine alternatives. This paper develops a conservative, market-constrained model of tobacco harm reduction (THR) that treats switching from cigarettes to non-combustible nicotine products as a function of legality, affordability, and supply readiness rather than education alone. Using global smoking-attributable mortality estimates and income-weighted measures of market feasibility, we estimate that feasible adoption of safer nicotine products could avert approximately 0.17-0.29 million deaths per year under a cautious switching scenario, 0.35-0.58 million under a moderate scenario, and 0.58-0.97 million under an ambitious but realistic scenario. Over a 40-year horizon with gradual adoption, these ranges correspond to roughly 6-10 million, 12-21 million, and 20-34 million deaths averted, respectively. Sensitivity analysis shows that plausible variation in the relative risk of non-combustible products has only a modest effect on outcomes. By contrast, regulatory and market constraints dominate results. The findings suggest that global tobacco control has largely exhausted the benefits of further education and now faces a structural failure to enable safer substitution at scale.

title: The Scale-up Pathway of China's Photovoltaic Industry: A Talent-Capital-Policy Coupling Framework

detail.title: The Scale-up Pathway of China's Photovoltaic Industry: A Talent-Capital-Policy Coupling Framework
detail.abstract: China's photovoltaic (PV) industry has grown from virtually nothing to dominating over 80% of global production capacity in less than two decades, whilst European and American industries have declined dramatically. This study proposes the "talent-capital-policy coupling mechanism" as a theoretical framework for explaining industrial scale-up success. We conceptualise "coupling" as the dynamic co-evolutionary interaction among elements generating synergistic effects beyond simple complementarity. Through comparative analysis of China, Europe, and America, we find that China's success results from effective temporal coupling of three elements: core talent's leading effect, broad patient capital, and policy continuity exemplified by Five-Year Plans. European and American industries failed through distinct coupling failures—breakdown through policy discontinuity in Europe, and non-formation through structural barriers in America—requiring distinct remediation strategies: trust rebuilding for Europe, structural reform for America.. This study further develops the "Industrial Scale-up Double Helix Model" as a visualisation framework with diagnostic power to identify element states and connection patterns. The contribution lies in revealing the "methodology" rather than merely the "outcome" of successful scale-up, providing theoretical guidance for emerging industry development.

title: The Household Impact of Generative AI: Evidence from Internet Browsing Behavior

detail.title: The Household Impact of Generative AI: Evidence from Internet Browsing Behavior
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of generative AI on U.S. households' task allocation at home, using detailed Internet browsing data from a large sample of home devices between 2021 and 2024. Leveraging pre-ChatGPT browsing patterns, we measure households' exposure to ChatGPT and use it as an instrument for ChatGPT adoption during the post-release period. Our IV estimates show that adopting generative AI substantially increases leisure browsing on home devices while leaving time spent on productive digital tasks unchanged. To examine mechanisms, we infer the purpose of households' ChatGPT use from surrounding internet activity and find that households primarily employ it for productive non-market tasks. Together, these results suggest that generative AI frees up leisure time by raising the efficiency of productive digital activities. Interpreting these findings through a standard model of time allocation, we find that they imply economically large productivity gains from generative AI at home.

detail.abstract: The accelerating pace of digital transformation within the airline industry necessitates a strategic reevaluation of data analytics practices, particularly the implementation of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for enhancing operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, and financial performance. This study delves into the strategic significance of KPIs in the realm of airline data analytics, employing a mixed-methods research design that includes literature review, expert interviews, and case studies of leading airlines. The findings underscore the transformative impact of data analytics across operational, customer, and financial dimensions, highlighting the critical role of aligning KPIs with strategic goals, fostering a data-driven organizational culture, and adapting KPI strategies in response to evolving technological and market dynamics. Furthermore, the research presents actionable recommendations for Data Analysis Directors and airline executives, advocating for continuous adaptation and strategic refinement of data analytics practices. This study contributes to both theoretical and practical understandings of strategic data analytics in the airline industry, offering a comprehensive guide for leveraging KPIs to achieve competitive advantage and operational excellence. Future research avenues are suggested, including the exploration of emerging data technologies and the ethical use of data, to further enhance the strategic application of KPIs in the airline industry.

title: Territorial Acquisition after 1945: The Legal Significance of the Gwadar Transfer

detail.title: Territorial Acquisition after 1945: The Legal Significance of the Gwadar Transfer
detail.abstract: The prohibition of the use of force and the right of self-determination have reshaped the law of territorial cession, expansion and acquisition. Before the United Nations Charter was adopted, state practice permitted the exchange of territories on the basis of financial consideration. In the post-1945 international order, territorial acquisitions continued to be a part of state practice, and was achieved through good offices, military restraint and joint resource management. The port of Gwadar was transferred from Oman to Pakistan. As questions arise over the future of Greenland, I examine how Gwadar was transferred. Self-determination has become an important qualifying criterion for territorial cession, which was affirmed in the Chagos Advisory Opinion. I link the ICJ's Nottebohm decision on determining citizenship with the right of self-determination. The joint management of oil fields on the Saudi-Kuwaiti border provides a further legal and regulatory precedent for shared sovereignty of resources.

title: Optimizing Astronomy Tourism Strategies A KPI-driven Approach to Enhancing Experience and Sustainability
