detail.abstract: The burgeoning niche of astronomy tourism presents a unique confluence of education, leisure, and environmental sustainability, poised for significant growth within the global tourism industry. This study explores the critical role of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) in optimizing the management, promotion, and development of astronomy tourism experiences. Employing a mixed-methods approach that combines quantitative data analysis with qualitative stakeholder insights, the research identifies pivotal KPIs across three main areas: Tourist Satisfaction Rates, Partnership Effectiveness, and Sustainability Measures. Findings highlight the Net Promoter Score (NPS) and repeat visitation rates as essential metrics for assessing customer satisfaction, while the impact of strategic partnerships and sustainability initiatives underscores the need for collaborative and environmentally responsible practices. This paper discusses the alignment of these findings with existing theories in tourism management and suggests practical strategies for practitioners to leverage KPIs for enhancing tourism experiences, promoting sustainability, and improving operational efficiency. Acknowledging certain limitations, including the scope of data collection, the study proposes directions for future research, emphasizing the expansion of KPI scope, cross-cultural consumer behavior exploration, and the economic impact analysis of astronomy tourism. This research contributes to the theoretical and practical understanding of managing astronomy tourism, offering insights into leveraging KPIs for strategic advantage in this niche yet rapidly evolving sector.

title: Spatial Heterogeneity in Pandemic Income Shocks and Safety Net Buffering: Evidence from California Labor Markets

detail.title: Spatial Heterogeneity in Pandemic Income Shocks and Safety Net Buffering: Evidence from California Labor Markets
detail.abstract: We examine how the COVID-19 pandemic affected household income across different types of California labor markets and assess the role of safety net programs in buffering income losses. Using IPUMS American Community Survey microdata from 2018-2023 linked to Labor Market Areas, we classify regions by pre-pandemic income levels and inequality. Our event study estimates document that nominal income gaps between high-cost and low-cost areas narrowed during the pandemic. However, when we adjust for local cost of living using the C2ER Cost of Living Index, a strikingly different picture emerges: low-income families in expensive metros like San Francisco and Los Angeles-who held a purchasing power advantage before COVID-ended up with lower real purchasing power than their rural counterparts by 2023. This reversal occurred because federal safety net programs distributed largely uniform dollar amounts regardless of local prices. A $1,400 stimulus check bought far more in Fresno than in San Francisco. Pre-trend analysis indicates that high-cost areas were already on a different income trajectory before the pandemic, so we interpret these patterns as descriptive evidence of spatial income dynamics rather than causal effects of COVID per se. Our findings suggest that geographically uniform benefit structures, while administratively simple, may inadvertently exacerbate spatial inequality in real terms.

title: The Speed of Corporate Cash Adjustment: Evidence from Labor Protection Laws
affiliations: Loughborough University - Loughborough Business School, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business,  and Loughborough University - Loughborough Business School

detail.title: The Speed of Corporate Cash Adjustment: Evidence from Labor Protection Laws
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of U.S. state-level labor protection laws on the speed of corporate cash adjustment. Exploiting the staggered adoption of wrongful discharge laws, we find that stronger labor protections significantly slow this adjustment, indicating greater frictions in rebalancing. The effect is asymmetric and particularly pronounced for cash-rich firms making downward adjustments. We identify three underlying mechanisms: intensified agency problems, heightened financial distress, and tightened financial constraints. Overall, our findings demonstrate that analyzing the speed of adjustment, rather than just cash levels, offers a more complete understanding of corporate cash policy.

title: What is the Value of Censored Data? An Exact Analysis for the Data-driven Newsvendor
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: What is the Value of Censored Data? An Exact Analysis for the Data-driven Newsvendor
detail.abstract: We study the offline data-driven newsvendor problem with censored demand data. In contrast to prior works where demand is fully observed, we consider the setting where demand is censored at the inventory level and only sales are observed; sales match demand when there is sufficient inventory, and equal the available inventory otherwise. We provide a general procedure to compute the exact worst-case regret of classical data-driven inventory policies, evaluated over all demand distributions. Our main technical result shows that this infinite-dimensional, non-convex optimization problem can be reduced to a finite-dimensional one, enabling an exact characterization of the performance of policies for any sample size and censoring levels. We leverage this reduction to derive sharp insights on the achievable performance of standard inventory policies under demand censoring. In particular, our analysis of the Kaplan-Meier policy shows that while demand censoring fundamentally limits what can be learned from passive sales data, just a small amount of targeted exploration at high inventory levels can substantially improve worst-case guarantees, enabling near-optimal performance even under heavy censoring. In contrast, when the point-of-sale system does not record stockout events and only reports realized sales, a natural and commonly used approach is to treat sales as demand. Our results show that policies based on this sales-as-demand heuristic can suffer severe performance degradation as censored data accumulates, highlighting how the quality of point-of-sale information critically shapes what can, and cannot, be learned offline.

title: Revolution Versus Evolution in Corporation Law: The ALI’s Project and the Independent Director

publicationDetails.detailsText: GMU Working Paper in Economics Vol 52, No 4
publicationDetails.journalName: George Mason University Department of Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Some of the most controversial proposals of the American Law Institute’s Corporate Governance Project relate to changes in the structure and composition of the board of directors. The initial proposal of the Principles of Corporate Governance and Structure: Restatement and Recommendations mandated that a majority of the directors of large publicly held corporations be outsiders. This proposal was subsequently amended to recommend that corporations select such a board as a matter of corporate practice. The debate about the structure and composition of the board and board committees continues among legal commentators. The desirability of governmental or quasi-governmental interference with organizational behavior in a free market  and an absence of evidence about the effect independent directors have on corporate performance lie at the heart of the debate. This Article attempts to fill the evidentiary void.

Part I introduces the legal and economic issues of the corporate governance debate and of the ALI’s Project. Part II discusses the functions of the board of directors and demonstrates that the board occupies a central position in both legal and economic perspectives on corporate governance. Current economic analysis suggests that the board’s existence is consistent with the evolutionary success of the corporation as an organizational form. Legal scholars, on the other hand, view the board as a potentially valuable element of a comprehensive system of corporate governance but argue that the entrenched central management of large American corporations has not allowed boards to function in this capacity. The controversy over the current role and efficacy of the board suggests the need for empirical analysis. 

Part III presents empirical evidence concerning the changing composition of the corporate board and the effect of such changes on corporate performance. Board independence increased during the 1970s as boards were staffed voluntarily by directors who would meet the ALI’s standard for independence. Apparently, the evolution occurred because senior management recognized a positive relationship between board independence and improved financial performance. Evidence indicates, however, that the revolutionary and intrusive changes advocated by some commentators could easily threaten corporate survival and that the present optimal degree of independence is well below the level proposed by the ALI’s Project. Part IV discusses the policy implications of this evidence.

detail.abstract: Standard financial analysis typically treats corporate governance as a compliance attribute or a lagging indicator of firm performance. This paper proposes a structural re-definition, positing governance as a behavioural system comprising two independent variables: Value Creation Intent (VCI) and Governance Capability (Agility). By operationalizing these constructs through "Governance Feature Engineering"-a method of quantifying leadership behaviour-and mapping the S&P 500 over a tenyear period (2015-2024), this research demonstrates that governance behaviour predicts outcome volatility and strategic failure well before financial ratios deteriorate. The study isolates the "COVID Stress Test" (2020-2022), revealing a significant capital migration from "Convergence" (High Intent/High Agility) to "Overreach" (High Intent/Low Agility). The findings confirm that outcome dispersion is endogenous to governance behaviour; specifically, "Overreach" firms exhibited volatility levels 20x higher than their "Convergent" peers during the 2022 market correction, despite reporting identical median returns. This framework offers a diagnostic tool to identify institutional fragility during periods of liquidity-driven growth.

title: Understanding the Interplay of Formal Rules and Informal Norms in Women's Academic Career Advancement

detail.title: Understanding the Interplay of Formal Rules and Informal Norms in Women's Academic Career Advancement

contentType.other: Abridged version of a chapter from PhD dissertation

detail.abstract: This article examines the dynamic interplay of formal and informal institutions in shaping women's advancement to academic leadership. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 17 women in senior academic leadership positions across four Nigerian federal universities, this study explores how formal promotion processes and informal norms interact to influence women's career trajectories. The study focuses on women's lived experiences of promotion, from entry-level academic cadre to academic leadership positions, to uncover where along the pipeline they encounter ease or difficulty, and why. It particularly explores the extent informal institutions subvert the intent of formal policies, potentially undermining women's advancement, and in what ways do women respond or adapt to these conditions? The Nigerian case is used as a lens to illuminate broader patterns that resonate globally, while also retaining context-specific insights. Comparisons are drawn between universities with explicit gender equality policies and those without, to assess whether a formal commitment to gender equity makes a tangible difference in practice. By integrating a Feminist Institutionalist perspective (FI) with a Feminist Critical Discourse Analysis (FCDA), the study provides a nuanced account of how power and gender operate within academic institutions. The analysis highlights key informal mechanisms such as gendered bias in promotion evaluations, patronage networks, and normative expectations around gender roles, that influence promotion outcomes. It also showcases the strategies of resistance that women develop and how they navigate these resistances, illustrating a complementary interplay of formal and informal institutions. Ultimately, this article argues that meaningful progress toward gender equity in academia requires not only robust formal policies but also cultural and institutional change that dismantles adverse informal norms. The findings contribute to debates on gender and higher education by shedding light on how hidden institutional dynamics and 'rules of the game' continue to affect women's leadership prospects, and what this implies for policy and practice in both Nigerian academia and globally.

Amidst the growing demand for sustainable and authentic travel experiences, this research aims to identify, analyze, and evaluate how specific KPIs can enhance the effectiveness of agritourism strategies, focusing on optimizing visitor experience, financial performance, operational efficiency, and sustainability. Employing a mixedmethods research design, the study combines qualitative analyses of case studies and expert interviews with quantitative evaluation of performance data across several agritourism operations. The findings highlight the critical role of KPIs in guiding strategic decision-making, with particular emphasis on customer experience metrics, financial indicators, operational metrics, and sustainability measures. The research illustrates that a KPI-driven approach is indispensable for achieving strategic agility, enhancing visitor satisfaction, and promoting sustainable practices within agritourism. Conclusively, the study not only contributes to the theoretical literature on agritourism and strategic management but also offers practical guidelines for agritourism operators seeking to navigate the complexities of integrating agriculture and tourism successfully.

title: Coercive Resource Diplomacy: Modeling China's Rare Earth Export Control Escalation Dynamics And Western Deterrence Options

detail.title: Coercive Resource Diplomacy: Modeling China's Rare Earth Export Control Escalation Dynamics And Western Deterrence Options

detail.abstract: This study investigates China's use of rare earth element (REE) export controls as instruments of coercive resource diplomacy and evaluates Western deterrence options through a mixed-methods research design integrating event study analysis, process-tracing case studies, and game-theoretic modeling. China's dominance over the rare earth supply chain—controlling approximately 60% of global mining and 90% of processing capacity—has created strategic vulnerabilities for Western nations dependent on these critical minerals for defense systems, clean energy technologies, and advanced manufacturing. Drawing on economic statecraft theory (Baldwin, 1985; Drezner, 2003), deterrence frameworks (Schelling, 1966; Morgan, 2003), and weaponized interdependence literature (Farrell & Newman, 2019), this research examines four empirical cases: the 2010 Japan embargo, the 2012-2014 WTO dispute period, the 2023-2025 graduated export control escalation, and the November 2025 diplomatic pause. Quantitative analysis of 25 policy events reveals significant cumulative abnormal returns for Western rare earth producers, including +29.36% for MP Materials following October 2025 MOFCOM controls and -39.11% for Lynas Rare Earths following diplomatic resolution announcements. Trade flow analysis documents $9.9 billion in Chinese rare earth exports to the United States, Japan, and European Union between 2010 and 2024, with Japan representing the largest import partner. Price volatility analysis indicates highest market disruption during the 2011-2014 WTO dispute period, with strong correlation (r = 0.85) between trade values and strategic rare earth prices. All four research hypotheses receive empirical support, demonstrating that export controls generate significant market reactions, escalation follows predictable patterns, Western resilience moderates coercion effectiveness, and diplomatic resolutions impact market expectations. The findings contribute to economic statecraft theory by documenting the "coercion paradox" whereby restrictions accelerate Western diversification efforts, ultimately undermining long-term Chinese leverage. Policy implications address optimal deterrence configurations for policymakers, industry stakeholders, and alliance coordination mechanisms.

title: Beyond Competitive Advantage: Large Understanding Models, Symbiotic Strategy, and a New Paradigm in Strategic Management

detail.title: Beyond Competitive Advantage: Large Understanding Models, Symbiotic Strategy, and a New Paradigm in Strategic Management
detail.abstract: Contemporary strategic thinking is at a crossroads. The classical paradigm of sustainable competitive advantage – long predicated on protected market positions and firm-specific resources – is increasingly challenged by an environment of blurring boundaries, digital interconnectivity, and rapid innovation. This conceptual paper critically examines why the canonical theory of competitive advantage has become epistemologically outdated in the 21st century. In its place, we propose a new paradigm centered on Large Understanding Models (LUMs) as a transformative lens for strategic management, organizational decision science, and AI-informed leadership theory. LUMs – introduced in the author’s prior work – integrate semantic comprehension, causal reasoning, and contextual intelligence within AI systems, enabling organizations to interpret complexity and make decisions with unprecedented depth. We frame LUMs as an original theoretical contribution, already being operationalized through the EU-based project Predictores.ai, thus bridging theory and practice. Further, drawing on Professor Chen Chunhua’s symbiotic strategy concept – encapsulated in her call to move from “closed fortresses” to “symbiotic interfaces” – we synthesize how a symbiotic, ecosystem-based view of strategy harmonizes with LUM-driven intelligence. The result is a novel perspective in which firms leverage understanding (both human and machine) as the central source of strategic value, rather than static competitive positions. We outline how LUMs reshape the interpretive capacity of organizations, enhance decision-making processes, and demand new leadership models that blend human judgment with AI co-analysis. This paper is purely theoretical, offering a rigorous, interdisciplinary framework that provocatively rethinks strategy in the AI era. We conclude by highlighting implications for future research and practice, positing that understanding-based strategy may eclipse traditional competitive advantage as the guiding logic of organizational success.

title: Which Companies are Ahead in Frontier Innovation on Critical Technologies? Comparing China, The European Union and the United States
affiliations: Bruegel, Bruegel and Bruegel

detail.title: Which Companies are Ahead in Frontier Innovation on Critical Technologies? Comparing China, The European Union and the United States
detail.abstract: Competition in critical technologies is attracting increasing attention not only because of the foundational nature of these technologies for other types of innovation, but also because of their role in the United States national security strategy. In this paper, we look into which entities in China, the European Union and the US innovate at the technology frontier in the three most important critical technologies-artificial intelligence, quantum computing and semiconductors-based on identification of the most radical novel patents in these technologies and their subsectors. Working with these pathbreaking patents, we look into the origin of the companies that file the largest numbers of them. US innovators dominate the innovation frontier for quantum computing and, to a lesser extent, AI, with Chinese innovators doing better in semiconductors. European innovators lag in all, but perform relatively better in quantum computing, in which they rank similarly to Chinese innovators. Furthermore, the innovation ecosystem is quite different across geographies. In the US, tech companies top the rankings of critical novelties and are highly concentrated: as many as three companies are in the top rankings of all of the three critical technologies. Frontier innovators in the field in which the EU competes most equally-quantum-are mostly research centres and not companies. China lies somewhat in between in all three domains.

title: How Similar is the Chinese Economy to that of Japan after the Bubble Burst?
affiliations: Bruegel

detail.title: How Similar is the Chinese Economy to that of Japan after the Bubble Burst?
detail.abstract:
Since the burst of China’s real estate sector bubble in mid2021, there is a growing concern that the Chinese economy could end up like that of Japan in the early 1990s. Some patterns are strikingly similar, such as the sharp deceleration in fixed asset investment, especially in the housing market. 

Both countries have long suffered from low private consumption, especially when compared with the rest of the world, and an excessively high saving ratio. Their initial policy responses to the growth challenges are also similar since both China and Japan were initially hesitant to ease monetary and fiscal policies after the collapse of the bubble. Instead, they chose to expand supply, in particular manufacturing, with an eye on external demand. The result of such policies is protracted trade surpluses, which did not help mitigate the consequences of the burst of the bubble. On the contrary, they only fed deflationary pressures. 

China seems to be following Japan in terms of seeking expansion of its overseas assets although with some differences. For Japan, offshoring or production to China and Southeast Asia, through greenfield foreign direct investment (FDI) was crucial in reducing its production costs and ensuring continued access to Western markets. The strategy also helped Japan circumventing protectionist measures, especially from the US. China has also stepped up its outbound investment, as Japan did in the 1980s although the focus has been a bit different, namely acquiring resources and building infrastructure through the Belt and Road Initiative. Another similarity to maintain supply has been the quest to move up the ladder, with a surge in expenditure in research and development (R&D). 

Notwithstanding the similarities, there are also crucial differences in China’s and Japan’s structural situation. Some should make China’s case potentially better off, but others push in the opposite direction. Starting with the latter, China’s macroeconomic imbalances, in particularly the excess saving and low private consumption, are much larger than that were in Japan and. China's reliance on manufacturing is also significantly larger, which has led to a larger share of global exports. 

Moreover, the wave of protectionism now is much stronger than it was when Japan was pushing its manufacturing in the 1980s. China will find it harder to protect itself from protectionism by offshoring its manufacturing capacity through greenfield investment than Japan did, especially because its income per capita are lower than those of Japan when it moved its production overseas in the 1980s. The positive angle for China, compared to Japan, is its geopolitical power with the Global South and its ability to become self-reliant technologically. This also offers options for China to create its own ecosystem if the US keeps containing China.

All in all, China seems to be heading to similar growth trajectory as Japan did in the past. However, some differences also exist that could yield different outcomes, making it important to closely monitor the situation.

detail.abstract:
This study explores the historical and contemporary implications of democratic imperial structures in Africa. Researchers adopted a structured approach, gathering and analysing qualitative data from a wealth of online literature sources and expert opinions. They meticulously selected 28 peer-reviewed articles spanning from 1958 to 2023, each discussing the Deconstructing Democratic Imperial Structures in African History. The data revealed the limitations of the growth of uncertainty to govern institutions in African countries. The systematic approach ultimately provided valuable insights into the struggles and challenges faced by the Deconstructing Democratic Imperial Structures in African History. By deconstructing the concept of democratic imperialism, the study highlights the ways in which external influences ranging from colonial rule to modern neo-colonial practices have shaped political institutions, social hierarchies, and economic systems in African nations. The research identifies three key themes: the legacy of colonial governance, the role of international organisations in promoting democratic values, and the impact of local resistance movements. Each theme underscores the tension between imposed democratic ideals and the realities of governance in diverse cultural contexts. Furthermore, the paper examines case studies from various African countries, illustrating how historical narratives are crucial for understanding current political challenges faced by many nations.

Ultimately, this study argues that a comprehensive understanding of Africa’s democratic trajectory necessitates a critical engagement with its imperial past. By incorporating voices from diverse scholarly perspectives, this research contributes to a nuanced discourse on democracy, sovereignty, and identity in Africa. The findings advocate for a re-evaluation of democratic frameworks that genuinely reflect the aspirations of African societies, thereby fostering more equitable and inclusive governance models.

This document presents the research design, theoretical motivation, and empirical strategy underlying the project. Expanded econometric results and replication materials are under preparation for peer-reviewed journal submission.

detail.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Equitable AI Integration through Teacher Empowerment

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping education through personalized learning, predictive analytics, and adaptive student support. However, its adoption in K-12 classrooms raises concerns about equity and teacher preparedness. This study explores how AI can advance equitable learning for students from diverse socioeconomic, cultural, and linguistic backgrounds, while highlighting the crucial role of teacher training in effective pedagogy. A qualitative method was used, involving semi-structured interviews with twelve educators from varied school settings. The research focuses on reducing disparities in access and enhancing teacher competency. Key challenges identified include the digital divide, affordability, potential algorithmic biases, data privacy, and the need for ongoing professional development. Thematic analysis of the data reveals that equitable AI integration depends on robust technological support and continuous teacher capacity building. Empowering educators to critically engage with AI enables inclusive, ethical, and accessible learning environments. This study aims to inform policies and practices that position AI as a tool for equity and innovation in modern education.

title: Green Building in India: Comparative Analysis of Five Leading Campuses
affiliations: , ,  and

detail.title: Green Building in India: Comparative Analysis of Five Leading Campuses
detail.abstract:
Sustainability in higher education institutions in India has moved from being optional to becoming a strategic priority. It is now closely linked with India’s climate commitments, including carbon neutrality, efficient use of resources, and responsible waste management. This study examines how Indian green building standards—GRIHA (Green Rating for Integrated Habitat Assessment) and IGBC (Indian Green Building Council)—influence sustainability outcomes on academic campuses.

Five leading campuses—IIT Madras, IIT Kharagpur, IIT Hyderabad, TERI University, and IIM Ahmedabad—were studied using secondary data. Metrics included certifications, waste management, water conservation, and renewable energy generation.

The results show strong progress in integrating sustainability into campus planning, especially through solar energy, wastewater treatment, and waste segregation. Institutions with GRIHA or IGBC certifications show more comprehensive environmental practices. Flagship campuses lead in renewable energy and water systems and are quick to adopt innovative technologies.

title: Does a Charitable Element Blend Well with a Monetary Incentive in the Commercial Recycling Market? A Large-Scale Quasi-Experiment
affiliations: Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, , Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Does a Charitable Element Blend Well with a Monetary Incentive in the Commercial Recycling Market? A Large-Scale Quasi-Experiment
detail.abstract: Various psychological factors encourage sustainable consumer behavior, but monetary incentives remain among the most effective approaches in practice for recycling. While incorporating charitable elements is an attractive option, doing so may conflict with the monetary incentives. We examine how the charitable element affects people’s recycling activities in the commercial recycling market. Using data from a commercial recycling network in China, we show that adding a charitable, autonomy-supportive option—allowing residents to choose whether to keep their monetary reward or donate it to a community project—significantly increases recycling activities both during and after the campaign period. On average, weekly recycling orders rose by 37% and total recycled weight by 87% during the campaign, and these effects persisted afterward. A significant portion of the increase came from residents who had not recycled before, suggesting that the campaign attracted a new segment motivated by either social values or the more autonomy-supportive incentive structure. In addition, although only a small portion of residents donated during the fundraising campaign, their subsequent recycling activities significantly increased afterward. Overall, our findings reveal that when monetary and charitable incentives are aligned and autonomy supportive, they can enhance participation and promote long term sustainable behavior in commercial recycling.

title: Gen Z's Expectations of Brand Responsibility: Navigating Social Justice, Mental Health and Sustainability
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Gen Z's Expectations of Brand Responsibility: Navigating Social Justice, Mental Health and Sustainability
detail.abstract:
Generation Z (Gen Z) is a socially conscious and digitally savvy consumer segment that is becoming more and more focused on the brand's commitment to social justice, mental health support, and sustainability. However, despite increased corporate interest in socially responsible practices, little research exists explaining how the three of these dimensions affect Gen Z's understanding of brand authenticity and trust in a unified way. This study addresses this gap by discussing about the responsible brand actions and how responsible actions affect the authenticity and authenticity leads to the prediction of trust among Gen Z consumers in Bengaluru.

A quantitative and cross-sectional research design was adopted, a structured questionnaire was used with the sample size of 300 Gen Z respondents being between the ages of 18-28 years. Multi-item Likert scales were created and used to measure Social Justice Engagement, Mental Health Support, Sustainability Practices, Perceived Brand Authenticity and Brand Trust. Data was analysed by the structural equation modelling (SmartPLS 4) on reliability, validity, direct effects, and mediation relationships.

Findings indicate that all three dimensions of brand responsibility have a significant, positive effect on perceived brand authenticity with sustainability practices being the most effective. Perceived brand authenticity became a very powerful predictor of brand trust. Mediation analysis confirmed some partial mediating effect of authenticity between the dimensions of responsibility and trust, pointing to the suggestion that the reason why Gen Z trusts brands is not only because of the responsible action, but because of the authenticity of the action and its communication.

The findings underscore the importance of authenticity as a key mechanism by which brands are connected to trust formation among Gen Z. Brands seeking to build strong and valuable relationships with young consumers must show consistent, transparent and long-term commitments to social and environmental issues. The research provides some practical information to marketers who are trying to create meaningful, honest branding strategies which will fit in with Gen Z's ethical expectations.

title: A Phenomenology of Rest
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Phenomenology of Rest
detail.abstract:
Rest is commonly associated with inactivity or withdrawal from ordinary demands. Yet this understanding does not align fully with experience. Extended holidays often fail to be restful, periods of inactivity can give rise to ennui, while certain ongoing activities—such as hobbies, gardening, music, or familiar craft—are frequently experienced as deeply restful despite requiring effort and attention. This paper seeks to understand why.

Rather than treating rest as the absence of activity, the paper examines a form of rest that occurs through activity. In these cases, agency remains active: one chooses, attends, corrects, and persists. To make sense of this, the paper analyses rest phenomenologically through the structure of agency. The analysis articulates the modern experience of restful activity as it is lived: contentment, ease, and fidelity.

The paper shows that this form of rest does not depend on reduced effort or disengagement, but on how the agent perceives and relates the real and the ideal. Certain activities are experienced as restful when agency remains active without being pulled forward toward improvement, outcome, or verdict. This account helps explain why regular hobbies can be more reliably restful than extended getaways.

title: Lifecycle Carbon Footprint Comparison Between Mass-Produced Electric Vehicles And Conventional Internal Combustion Vehicles
affiliations: and AIT Austrian Institute of Technology GmbH

detail.title: Lifecycle Carbon Footprint Comparison Between Mass-Produced Electric Vehicles And Conventional Internal Combustion Vehicles
detail.abstract: This study quantifies and compares the lifecycle carbon footprints of mass-produced electric vehicles (EVs) and conventional internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) across representative vehicle classes and market regions. Using a standardized cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment (LCA) framework, we integrate manufacturing (including battery production), fuel and electricity supply chains, vehicle use phase, maintenance, and end-of-life treatments (recycling, remanufacture, disposal). Scenarios account for variability in electricity grid carbon intensity, vehicle lifetime mileage, fleet vehicle energy efficiency, battery chemistry and production location, and recycling recovery rates. Results show that, under present average grid mixes in major markets, EVs produce lower total CO2-equivalent emissions over typical lifetimes for most vehicle segments, with the magnitude of advantage strongly conditioned by grid decarbonization and battery manufacturing emissions. In high-carbon grids and for short vehicle lifetimes, the EV lifecycle advantage is reduced or can be negated; conversely, in low-carbon grids and with high battery recycling rates, EVs deliver substantial lifecycle reductions (often exceeding 50% for compact and midsize segments). Sensitivity and uncertainty analyses reveal battery production emissions, annual vehicle kilometers travelled, and electricity mix as the most influential parameters. Policy implications include prioritizing rapid grid decarbonization, improving battery manufacturing efficiency and supply chain transparency, and expanding battery reuse and recycling infrastructure to maximize EV lifecycle benefits. The findings inform manufacturers, policymakers, and fleet operators by identifying the conditions under which electrification yields meaningful carbon reductions and by highlighting strategic levers to accelerate net emissions avoidance.

title: A Phenomenology of Flow
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Phenomenology of Flow
detail.abstract:
Contemporary concern with productivity has foregrounded the phenomenon of flow across creative and technical work. Flow is widely discussed and frequently sought as a condition in which effort moves smoothly and activity feels coherent rather than strained. Yet despite its prominence, flow remains elusive—more often described or retrospectively recognised than reliably sustained.

This paper examines flow through the structure of an agency cycle, focusing on how it is experienced by the individual rather than inferred from external performance. It identifies three minimal capabilities required for flow to occur and articulates the distinctive phenomenologies that arise when these capabilities align.

The paper argues that common approaches to flow, particularly those centred on productivity techniques or environmental optimisation, are structurally limited. Instead, it proposes that *flow* depends on a specific orientation to action—one that also explains why flow is easily disrupted and frequently misunderstood.

title: Navigating Environmental Compliance: Maritime Fleet Renewal Under Fuel Market Uncertainty
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Navigating Environmental Compliance: Maritime Fleet Renewal Under Fuel Market Uncertainty

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Singapore Maritime Institute (SMI) Fellowship award (SMI-2023-FS-02)

detail.abstract: International shipping is entering a period in which fleet investment, fuel-market development, and climate regulation must be managed jointly. We study long-horizon fleet renewal planning for a liner company facing tightening decarbonization targets and uncertain alternative-fuel markets. We develop a ship-resolved optimization model that coordinates discrete renewal actions (energy-efficiency retrofits, dual-fuel conversions, and end-of-life replacement) with annual fuel deployment across compatible fuels, subject to ship-level technology constraints and fleetwide caps on low-/zero-carbon fuel availability. Regulatory compliance is represented through a modular mapping that captures fuel-intensity standards with deficit payments, surplus crediting, and targeted rewards for eligible fuels, enabling comparison across regulatory architectures. We solve a deterministic model under given fuel cost and supply trajectories and a scenario-based stochastic extension in which near-term retrofit choices are made before fuel-market conditions are revealed, to examine how fuel markets and regulation jointly shape decision strategies. Numerical study on an Asia--Europe liner service shows that limited low-carbon fuel availability is a first-order constraint: cost-optimal pathways shift toward efficiency everywhere, with scarce low-carbon volumes targeted to ships with longer remaining life, and continued reliance on compliance-unit purchases during the transition. Under a hybrid regulatory environment and fuel scarcity, allocating limited volumes to keep more ships near a Base target is often preferred to pushing a few ships into surplus-credit regions. Explicit uncertainty modeling yields a more selective, hedged early retrofit portfolio than mean-trajectory planning, delivering modest expected-cost gains but materially lower downside risk. Finally, standard-based regulatory designs induce earlier technology commitment and sustained fuel switching, while a pure levy can yield persistent emissions payments with weaker structural decarbonization when the price signal declines, highlighting the role of standards and incentives in shaping transition pathways.

title: A Phenomenology of Failure
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Phenomenology of Failure
detail.abstract:
This paper is a phenomenological account of failure, examined through the lens of agency. It describes failure as a condition in which action remains answerable to an intent, while experience no longer revises expectation.

The analysis articulates the modern experience of failure as it is lived: narrowing possibility (despair), effort that does not accumulate (futility), and forms of functioning that stabilise activity while preventing revision (pathological stability). These experiences are traced across a canonical example of skill acquisition and a series of parallel cases drawn from work, responsibility, and practice.

The aim of the paper is diagnostic. It seeks to shed light on the experience of failure by offering a systematic phenomenological lens to sit alongside classical accounts of error, learning, and resilience. By rendering the structure of failure legible, the paper leaves judgement about effort, revision, or abandonment to the agent.

detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study investigates Turkey's emergence as a cryptocurrency transit corridor for Iranian sanctions evasion. It identifies the principal evasion typologies, estimates corridor transaction volumes, and proposes a compliance framework for virtual asset service providers (VASPs) and financial institutions with Turkish exposure.

Design/methodology/approach – The study employs a mixed-methods design combining doctrinal legal analysis of Turkish, Iranian, U.S., and international regulatory instruments with empirical blockchain forensics. Quantitative data derive from the Nation-State Crypto Threat Intelligence Platform (NSCTIP), covering January 2020 through December 2024. Volume estimates use a three-tier attribution confidence methodology (confirmed, high, medium) and are presented with conservative, base, and upper-bound scenarios.

Findings – Three primary evasion typologies are documented: stablecoin-based trade settlement, mining revenue monetization, and nested exchange services. Base-case corridor volume estimates grew from approximately $0.9 billion (2020) to $5.8 billion (2024 Q1–Q3). Regulatory fragmentation between Turkish supervisory authorities creates exploitable gaps. OFAC enforcement actions increasingly feature Turkish nodes in Iranian evasion networks.

Research limitations/implications – Blockchain attribution is probabilistic; volume estimates represent plausible ranges rather than precise measurements. The NSCTIP platform is author-developed, and independent replication with alternative analytics tools would strengthen confidence in the findings.

Practical implications – The compliance framework provides actionable detection indicators, blockchain analytics requirements, and enhanced due diligence protocols specifically calibrated for Turkish-corridor sanctions evasion risk.

Originality/value – To the author's knowledge, this study represents one of the most detailed open-source typological analyses of the Turkey–Iran crypto corridor, drawing on five years of systematically collected blockchain forensic data.

title: Engagement-Dependent Utility: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: University of Toronto and University of Toronto

detail.title: Engagement-Dependent Utility: Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract: A student who expects a college course to be worthwhile may pay close attention and learn a great deal, while a student who expects that course to be a waste of time may scroll through their phone during class and learn nothing. The quality of the lecture is the same for each, but their realized utility is different due to their (belief-induced) engagement level. We develop a model in which consumers choose engagement with a product based on beliefs about product quality and where engagement affects the distribution of realized utility. We then provide evidence on this mechanism in a large-scale experiment with over 500 book readers, recruited from online reader communities and randomly assigned novels to read, with a subset randomly assigned to view reviews before reading. We show that negative reviews reduce both expectations and realized enjoyment: readers shown bad reviews are 15 percentage points less likely to report above-average expectations and 11 percentage points less likely to report above-average enjoyment. This negative effect on enjoyment is driven by a compression of the enjoyment distribution, with lower density of both high ratings and very-low ratings, and sustains over the course of reading, with bad-review exposed readers showing declining trajectories of enjoyment while control readers show increasing trajectories. We estimate a structural model from our experimental data and, through stylized simulations, illustrate how the realized utility and average ratings of products can be shaped by different marketing strategies in this framework.

title: The Boomer Asset Mirage: A Cohort Asset Circularity Trap

detail.title: The Boomer Asset Mirage: A Cohort Asset Circularity Trap
detail.abstract:
Prevailing analyses of the generational wealth transfer from Baby Boomers (born 1946–1964) to younger cohorts project a nominal transfer of $70 to $100 trillion over the next two decades. This paper argues that these estimates are structurally overstated because they fail to account for the role the boomer cohort plays in sustaining the value of the assets it holds.

We introduce the Boomer Asset Mirage framework and the concept of the Cohort Asset Circularity Trap: a condition in which asset values are partly a function of the continued existence and consumption behavior of the cohort holding them, such that the cohort’s exit simultaneously reduces the demand that sustained asset values while increasing supply. The trap operates through two interacting channels.

The real estate channel: boomers own approximately 37 percent of U.S. homes and an estimated 68–70 percent of the nation’s vacation home stock. As this cohort ages and dies, 20 to 30 million properties are projected to enter the market, concentrated in geographic areas — rural markets, aging suburbs, and Southern coastal vacation communities — where millennial demand is structurally insufficient to absorb supply at current valuations. Geographic mismatch, declining carrying-cost affordability, and climate-related insurance pressures compound the risk, particularly in second-home markets.

The equity channel: boomers hold approximately 54 percent of U.S. corporate equity and mutual fund assets, disproportionately concentrated in industries — pharmaceuticals, elder care, leisure travel, financial advisory services — that depend on boomer consumer demand. As the cohort declines, earnings outlooks in these sectors deteriorate concurrently with boomer liquidation of those holdings, creating a drawdown-deflation dynamic.

The paper further documents a macro backdrop: boomers drive an estimated 40 percent of U.S. consumer spending, equivalent to approximately 28 percent of GDP. Their demographic exit therefore carries aggregate demand implications that extend well beyond the asset classes they hold. A second-order financial system risk is identified in estate-driven foreclosures on encumbered vacation properties, with structural — though not mechanically equivalent — parallels to the geographic concentration dynamics of the 2007–2010 housing crisis.

We find that existing research addresses these dynamics in disciplinary fragments — housing supply, equity reallocation, and wealth concentration — without integrating the feedback mechanism that connects them. This paper proposes a unified framework and calls for an integrated empirical model incorporating regional housing supply dynamics, equity sector demand exposure, and cohort-level wealth concentration, which to the authors’ knowledge does not yet exist in the published literature.

title: Wage Theft, Reneging and Liquidity Constraints in Informal Labor Markets

detail.title: Wage Theft, Reneging and Liquidity Constraints in Informal Labor Markets
detail.abstract: Informal labor markets in low-and middle-income countries exhibit high unemployment and job turnover despite high labor demand. We conduct two field experiments to study how wage theft, worker reneging, and liquidity constraints generate a mismatch between workers' labor supply and firms' labor demand. In the first experiment, 1,360 workers receive real job offers on either flat/daily-pay contracts, which do not withhold wages and therefore reduce wage theft concerns and workers' liquidity constraints, or back-loaded contracts, which withhold wages and impose these constraints. Labor supply is around three times larger for flat/daily-pay contracts. This preference is driven by workers' fears of wage theft by firms, liquidity constraints, and a demand for flexibility to exit contracts. This flexibility protects workers from income losses following shocks or from excess work extraction by firms under back-loaded contracts. The costs of these frictions are high because 72% of workers who reject job offers subsequently earn less income than those offers would have provided. In the second experiment, we make real offers to hire workers on either flat/daily-pay or back-loaded contracts to 349 firms. Firms' labor demand almost doubles for back-loaded contracts and this is driven by liquidity constraints, transaction costs, and the costs of worker reneging under flat/daily-pay contracts. We then match firms and workers who accepted contracts in the first two experiments. In the matching stage, workers are 69% more likely to complete back-loaded contracts than flat/daily-pay contracts. Flat/daily-pay contracts have a 34% completion rate and thereby impose significant costs on firms. Firms extract longer working hours under backloaded contracts, consistent with workers' stated concerns.

title: The Wage and Mobility Effects of Remote Work
affiliations: ,  and Institut des politiques publiques (PSE)

detail.title: The Wage and Mobility Effects of Remote Work
detail.abstract: The shift to remote work, with roots predating Covid-19, marks a major transformation of labor markets. This paper investigates its medium-run impact on workers' labor market outcomes, exploiting plant-level variation in remote work agreements implemented between 2014 and 2017 in France. Using an event study design and rich administrative data, we find that access to remote work yields moderate wage increases and facilitates geographical mobility with increases in commuting distance. Examining mechanisms, we find that workers moving to new plants that also have adopted remote work experience larger increases in commuting distance, along with upward occupational mobility. This pattern suggests that remote work options alleviate job search constraints, allowing workers to seek higher-paying and possibly higher-ranked jobs. Our analysis further reveals that plant-level remote work agreements raise firm productivity, benefiting both incumbent and newly hired workers. Overall, our results underscore how remote work reshapes labor market trajectories through its effects on mobility, job search, and productivity.

title: Expertise and Prediction Accuracy
affiliations: Kreditanstalt für Wiederaufbau (KFW), Ifo Institute, Technische Universität München (TUM), , Ifo Institute and Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: Expertise and Prediction Accuracy
detail.abstract: Public support for policy interventions depends on citizens’ beliefs about their likely ef-fects. We examine how individuals form such beliefs by studying their predictions of experimental outcomes in a policy-relevant setting, and why their predictions differ from expert benchmarks. We elicit forecasts from 127 professional economists and a repre-sentative sample of 6,200 German households about a large-scale behavioral experi-ment on education policy (N = 3, 133). Non-experts predict both average outcomes and treatment effects far less accurately than experts. Prediction accuracy improves with calibrated priors, self-reported effort, and the use of structured reasoning, but remains well below expert levels. We show that scalable design features, including the provision of well-calibrated numerical anchors and monetary incentives to rise effort, improve non-expert predictions, with effects comparable in magnitude to tertiary education or structured reasoning. Our findings have important implications for bridging the ‘expertise gap’ in public discourse.
